That this House condemns the government for undermining the Canadian trucking industry through an irresponsible approach to deregulation, taxation, and Canada-U.S. trade, and;
That this House calls upon the government to introduce immediate measures to permit Canadian truckers to compete on a level playing field with their American counterparts.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased on behalf of my Liberal colleagues in the House of Commons today to make the subject of our opposition day motion the crisis facing the Canadian trucking industry, an industry that in terms of federal responsibility was placed on a very slippery slope in 1988 when the government, the national Conservative government, deregulated the trucking industry. Since then Canadian trucking firms have had to protest without any success, have had to urge blockades to try to get the attention of the government and, this week, those truckers have brought their concerns to Ottawa and have parked themselves in front of the Eternal Flame on Parliament Hill.

May 17, 1991
Supply
On Monday our Liberal caucus met those truckers and met the spouses and the children of those truckers to try to give them at least a forum for venting their frustrations that have come to the fore. We, through the parliamentary opportunities granted to us in Question Period, have tried to raise those concerns. We have also petitioned the Speaker for an emergency debate which was regrettably turned down.
Therefore we have gone the extra distance of dedicating this day for the concerns facing the national trucking industry in Canada.
Our concern did not start this week. Our concern has certainly been voiced in terms of the deregulated mode that the government is introducing in the transport sector, not only in trucking but elsewhere. Not only have members of Parliament met Canadian truckers in Ottawa, but members of the Liberal caucus have met with those trucking companies and representatives in major cities in Ontario and elsewhere. Members of Parliament from Windsor West, Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, Essex-Kent, Haldimand-Norfolk, the riding of Kent, Lambton-Middlesex, Willowdale, and Prince Edward- Hastings, just to name a few, and others have confronted the concerns of those Canadians.
Deregulation, 1988. To try to make the Canadian industry more competitive, to try to inject competition and efficiency, the government opened the doors of deregulation, and thereby allowed market forces to clearly dominate. Before deregulation, an American trucking firm had to prove that there was indeed a market requirement for that firm to do the hauling, given the fact that Canadian firms were not doing it. It could be appealed by Canadian interests so that if the market between Buffalo and Toronto was saturated, then for all intents and purposes that American firm would not be permitted in that saturated market.
Under deregulation, that market and those doors have been fully opened, and that has meant that American firms have had the license to freely come into our market and compete head to head. It has meant that in 1986, before deregulation, in the province of Ontario there were 500 trucking carriers trying to deal with a $2 billion freight business.
After deregulation there are 3,000 truckers after the same pie, and therefore the survival of the fittest has become the rules of the game. Since deregulation there have been almost a thousand companies-600 last year
alone-that have gone belly up and have gone under and are not returning.
This is not a small industry. It is an industry which employs directly over 600,000 Canadians, with indirect spin-offs. I would suggest to the minister, with regard to the seven famous studies, that the time for study ought to have been before the flood gates were opened, before the deregulated bam door was thrown open, to ascertain what the down sides and the up sides would be under deregulation. The deregulatory doors were opened and then the consequences were studied.
The government deregulated, allowing American companies to come in freely, and it did so knowing full well the realities of the trucking market: Canadian truckers would be forced to operate at a 15 to 20 per cent cost disadvantage; American truckers could write off their trucks in four years, while in Canada that same write-off takes 13 years. American truckers can write off their licences, Canadian truckers cannot. Fuel prices are comparatively 20 cents per litre more in Canada than in the United States. Buying a new track in the United States costs, on average, $70,000; in Canada $90,000. In addition, we have a high dollar and a high interest rate policy which further aggravate an already bad situation.
With the geographic nature of our country, it is very clear that the American trucking fraternity can penetrate most of our market very quickly and very easily through the cross borders. We simply cannot reciprocate because we would not be able to compete in the heartland of America and hit its far-flung markets. Our populations are sparse whereas those in the United States are certainly concentrated in greater numbers.
When we talk about buying tires, equipment and insurance, the Americans pay less. For example, to refit a set of tires on an average rig in the United States costs $2,500; in Canada, the same set of tires is $5,000. In Canada a tune-up for an average rig is double that of an American tune-up.
We have deregulation, then we have deregulation on a basis that the Canadian government knew exactly that the Canadian trucking company, unless it has an equalizer, unless it has an adjustment mechanism, would not be able to compete fairly and successfully head to head. Is it any wonder that those truckers, angered and frustrated with the economic realities of the marketplace, have parked their vans and trucks in front of Parliament Hill?
May 17, 1991

All that reflects the human face of the economic misery which is facing Canadian truckers. It is organized frustration of not only truckers but of other workers who have had enough of this government's policies. These policies are irresponsible and they are insensitive to the needs of Canadians. Canadian interests ought to be priority number one, not priority number two.
None of the Canadian trucking firms last year made sizeable profits. GTL, the fourth largest firm, whose head office is virtually next door in my colleague's riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, went under just last week.
In our meetings, we heard not only testimony from the drivers, but from their wives and children. They are hurting as well because spouses are being forced to take on two jobs to make ends meet at the end of the month because there is no money coming in. There are no jobs. There is no profit. There is no pride any more if the Canadian trucking industry is allowed to continue its slide down the slippery slope of deregulation.
Many wives told us in very emotional ways about the food rationing in their own families. They told us that many truckers do not have sick pay or holiday pay. When they take a day, it comes out of their wages. We met Dave Wallis, who before deregulation had seven rigs operating at profits.
Today, Dave Wallis has one truck left and he is on the verge of losing that last truck. Dave Wallis must pay $60 an hour to a mechanic to fix his rig but he can only get $30 an hour to haul the materials. How does a Dave Wallis survive? How long can Dave Wallis tread water?
The Dave Wallis is symptomatic. We need to talk about the Dave Wallis' of this country. Rather than hiding behind studies or generic terms, we need to discuss the impact on the average Canadian trucker. What is the impact on the average Canadian family in that business and in others?
It is not only a problem in the trucking industry. Talk about Open Skies. The government wants to deregulate
Supply
the skies. Is it going to do to our air carriers what it has done to our truck carriers?
Why does the government not ask the Americans to take down the protectionist walls in shipping? The Americans refuse to compete in shipping. They know that our Canadian shipping industry can compete very well, thank you very much. Oh no. The Americans do not want to ruin their industry.
They put up a wall there, but they tell this Canadian government to bring down the walls on trucking and in your skies so we can compete and do a job on you.
I also want to mention that the infrastructure of VIA Rail has been gutted. It is not only an isolated case of the trucking fraternity. It is a mindset that has been applied to the trucking industry and to the rail industry. It is being applied, perhaps, in the few short months now that the government is negotiating Open Skies, to our air carriers.
I think that the transport industry in this country is not only important economically, but it has been a sense of pride and a sense of unity in terms of the development of this country.
While no one should be an ideologue or dogmatic, we should also protect, preserve and try to promote our own transport industries rather than giving them away.
I would suggest to the hon. minister-I appreciate and thank him-who listened to our appeals to at least meet with the visiting delegation. He has done so and he has met for the last day or day and a half with these owner-operator truckers, which he had not done before. I appreciate the fact that he has given his hours to try to mediate.
The time for throwing out the word "study" is over. There are seven studies under way that may not report until the end of the summer. Canadian truckers need a greater sense of hope because his predecessor, in Windsor last year when the truckers did the same blockade, basically raised the expectations of the trucking community. The predecessor to this minister said: "Do not worry. I will talk to the Minister of Finance. I will put in place reforms that will try to equalize the level playing field between the United States and Canada".

May 17, 1991
Supply
What has happened is precious little. Therefore, the expectations are high. The stakes are high. Those stakes have been raised by the government. Therefore, I urge the minister to be very cognizant of what his predecessors have put in motion.
His predecessor even said in a letter that he would not be prepared to wait until the final seven studies are in before taking action. I think that this minister ought not to simply study the issue to death while jobs are dying, families are struggling and hope is dwindling.
I am going to suggest to the minister nine options that our caucus and our party are prepared to put on the floor of the House of Commons today for debate. Nine options that, either in whole or in part, I believe and my caucus and my leader believes can, in fact, be the immediate remedy to some of the challenges facing truckers.
Option number one is a quicker write-off provision under Revenue Canada. I have mentioned that the United States truckers can write a percentage of their truck off in four years, whereas, the Canadian trucker by comparison takes 13 years. I would suggest that Revenue Canada permit the Canadian truckers to write off their rigs between four to seven years, therefore, cutting the depreciation time in half and bringing it up to speed with the American truckers. A truck costs a lot of money and, therefore, a quicker write-off period would put more dollars in the pockets of Canadian truckers. It would add to the cash flow and would allow the trucker some latitude and some flexibility to meet the hard times. The hard times are here now and, therefore, there is a greater sense of urgency for cash flow during a recessionary time. That assistance is needed now.
Option two is to take a look at the federal excise tax and offer some relief in terms of diesel fuel. The taxes are both provincial and federal. I will come to the provincial one. The federal tax is roughly four cents per litre. However, the federal government ought to recognize that where the inequities really begin is in the base price. Diesel fuel in the United States, before tax, is 18.6 cents a litre. In Canada it is 37.9 cents. After tax in the United States it is 27 cents per litre and in Canada, after tax, 59 cents.
What I am suggesting is that, in terms of the federal tax, the government can have three options. It can provide a temporary relief on payment of the federal
excise tax until the industry is back on its fee. It can perhaps drop the excise tax by a cent or by a margin it feels would provide some leadership to the provincial transport ministers in the provinces to do likewise. This would show good faith and at the same time, of course, relieve the truckers from that.
Third, the government can also provide the truckers, as we do the farming community, with a subsidy on diesel fuel. Those are three possible options the government could implement to deal adequately and efficiently with the federal tax on diesel fuel.
Option number four relates to the GST. We believe the government should scrap the GST, period. However, it seems the government is going to persist with the GST. Therefore, we are suggesting, that the government drastically shorten the rebate period for Canadian truckers. Currently, truckers pay GST on fuel and then receive a rebate. It takes about six months. That period is far too long. Canadian truckers give money to the government, almost as a loan, and have to wait six months for their rebate. In that sue month period, compared to their American competition, the American driver is ahead.
The period for the rebate should be considerably shorter than six months. On average, to fill up the tank of a diesel truck costs $250 more in Canada than it does in the United States. Every fill-up costs the Canadian trucker $250 more. If truckers received their rebate in a shorter period of time that money would assist greatly in their cash-flow.
The other option related to the GST is that the government should provide the truckers with a longer period of time to pay the GST on the goods they ship and collect from the shipper. The problem is that this government requires the Canadian trucker to submit the GST collected from the shipper within 45 days but the shipper does not pay the trucking company for 50, 60 or 90 days. This means that truckers have to pay the GST on the goods shipped and their invoices do not get paid for 90 days. We have again money going out of the pockets of Canadian truckers.
We are suggesting as option number four that the government tiy to equalize the lag so that the Canadian trucker is not out of pocket. As soon as those invoices are paid then the GST would be remitted. This gives a

financial break, in terms of cash-flow, to Canadian truckers.
Option number five. We are suggesting that the government seriously consider allowing Canadian truckers to deduct their licence fees, their licence expenses. American truckers can deduct the licence fees from their taxes. Revenue Canada does not extend the same luxury to Canadian truckers. A licence fee, on average in Canada, costs $2,000. We are suggesting, therefore, to allow Canadian truckers, like the American trucking fraternity, to deduct those licence fees from their taxes.
Madam Speaker, you mentioned that I have a minute left. I seek the co-operation of the House to allow me to finish presenting my nine points so the government can respond.
Option number six. I would suggest that the federal Minister of Transport urgently convene a ministers' meeting of his provincial counterparts because, while there are two levels of government involved with trucking, there is one trucking constituency. That trucking constituency needs a coherent, co-ordinated and harmonized approach to deal with their problems. The federal government blames the NDP government of Ontario, and the NDP government, Premier Rae, blames the federal Conservative government. They are blaming each other and it is a great Ping-Pong game, but those truckers are still outside and still hurting.
We need an urgent meeting to co-ordinate our efforts and begin to deal with the problems head on.
Option number seven is to pursue a federal-provincial trade-off. What do I mean by that?
I am suggesting financial co-operation to ease the provincial tax portion, which is roughly 15 cents, a heavy burden, almost four times the federal tax. I believe that the federal government can encourage the provincial governments, of Ontario for example, to reduce the burden of their excise tax if it, for example, is flexible enough in terms of funding for infrastructure of roads.
In the United States, the national government pays roughly 20 to 25 per cent of road construction. In Canada the federal government pays 5 per cent and the majority is obviously paid by the provinces. The federal government should say: " If we consider increasing the moneys we will give to the provinces for construction of roads, will you, the provinces, give the truckers a bit of a break
Supply
on the excise tax?" What the provinces lose from their fuel excise tax, they will gain in transfer payments from the federal government for construction of roads.
Perhaps Mr. Rae in Ontario would not levy 2 cents, as he did in his budget, and another 2 cents on January 1, 1992. That is exorbitant. I believe there can be a constructive give and take between the two levels of government to the advantage of the Canadian trucker.
Option number eight. Many American truckers and American trucks are now engaging in illegal cabotage. That is a fancy way of saying that instead of going from Buffalo to Toronto and back from Toronto to Buffalo, those truckers are going from Buffalo to Toronto, sneaking into Hamilton, perhaps London, and then back into Buffalo. Canadian truckers cannot compete as it is. We are going to be thrown off the road if American truckers continue to engage in illegal cabotage because we cannot compete with them.
Option number eight contains two subsections. First, a greater enforcement mechanism at our border crossings to ensure that our enforcements may in fact be enforced and American truckers know clearly that we will come down hard and very quickly. I would suggest that the penalty, when an American trucker is found doing illegal cabotage, be increased immediately from a $2,000 fine to a $5,000 fine. This represents a doubling and gives it a bit more teeth. If an American trucker wants to take a chance, he will pay stiffer penalties if he is caught. Hopefully, he will be caught at the border crossings because of stricter enforcement. We have jurisdiction at the border crossings.
Option number nine is a temporary moratorium on new interprovincial licences to try to stand back until this industry has caught its breath. Ontario has done that for its new licences. It does not solve the problem of the existing licences, but it certainly does not aggravate it to the nth degree. In interprovincial trucking the federal government has jurisdiction, so it can impose that moratorium if it wants.
Madam Speaker, I appreciate your flexibility and the flexibility of my colleagues on the other side. I have tried to be constructive. I have tried to give some facts on what deregulation has done, how uncompetitive we are head to head and third, to offer nine options which I believe, if enacted in whole or in part or in combination, will allow those truckers outside to enjoy this holiday weekend just

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would also like to respond to what was said by the hon. member opposite. To hear him talk, he and his party have all the answers.
What often bothers me about the hon. member is that every time something happens on this side of the House in Ottawa, it is always because he recommended it. I have been watching the minister for the last few days, and I saw he managed to meet them and their families as well. I also met the truckers.
Madam Speaker, I used to work in the industry, and truckers really have problems. Those people outside really need help. I know them. I worked for them and with them, and I had the privilege of having them as customers. They are really in trouble.
My colleagues do not seem to realize what the situation is, and they seem to be proving it this morning. Fifteen years ago, we repaired trucks for these people. Believe it or not, some garages wouldn't do jobs for truckers because they couldn't pay the repair bills. That is a sad commentary, and these people certainly did not have an easy life.
I hardly think these people are here today because the situation has improved. In fact, they are getting the short end of the stick. There have been taxes, taxes and more taxes. They were taxed on diesel fuel, they were taxed on gas-they were taxed on just about everything.
There is another problem the hon. member forgot to mention. About five years ago, a company in my riding, owned by a good friend of mine, couldn't get insurance. He was paying $30,000 for a fleet of 20 trucks, and he was going to be charged $135,000 for going to the United States. He went to the United States because his company had business there.
And now with free trade, I thought he would keep going to the United States. But nothing has changed. So it isn't because of the GST. Fifteen years ago there was no GST. It isn't because of the GST, because five years
ago the GST didn't exist. There was a tax on gas, but not as high as it is now. Unfortunately, provincial taxes don't only hurt truckers-and I said so when Quebec brought down its latest provincial budget-they also tend to aggravate other problems, because truckers transport goods- consumer goods. It isn't the GST. Here in Quebec, it's the GST plus the QST, plus this and that. But people tend to forget that.
Earlier, the hon. member said there are solutions. There is no miracle solution! Even if we remove the GST tomorrow morning, the truckers might get from Wellington to the next street over, but the problem would still be there. There is no miracle solution. The minister made this quite clear. What we need is a package of solutions.
The Liberal Party's solution is quite simple: forward, reverse, forward and reverse. You don't do that when you drive a truck. You have eighteen forward gears and one reverse. Madam Speaker, I used to work for a company that had 3,500 trucks to repair. But the problem was always the same. I used to say-do I have a few minutes left, Madam Speaker?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since May 1990, groups of unaffiliated truck owner-operators have been sporadically demonstrating and blockading highway checkpoints.
Truckers' concerns have been focused on taxation differentials between Canada and the U.S., notably on fuel and on the enforcement in Canada of the prohibition of cabotage-the carrying of goods between Canadian points by U.S. trucks-and on the impact of economic regulatory reforms and free trade generally in the industry.
In the summer of 1990, my predecessor established a task force to look at the concerns expressed by the truckers and created a forum for dialogue. I venture to say that this is a much more productive direction than hearing the previous speaker, my hon. colleague from York West, say that a committee of the Liberal Party has been functioning throughout this year.
Today in the House of Commons he deposits on the floor nine quick-fix solutions in an area where there is no quick-fix solution. The solutions that we must look into are medium-term and long-term solutions.
In the summer of 1990, this task force was created. It includes representatives of major trucking associations,
union leaders, independent owner-operators and provincial government officials. This task force has initiated studies on taxation, trucking costs, cabotage and on other factors considered to affect the competitive position of the Canadian trucking industry.
The studies are expected to be ready for release at the end of this month.
Although some laws apply to interprovincial highway transport, provincial governments enforce the legislation and generally take the lead in this field. The situation today is that there is a task force process under way with representatives of all segments of the industry, with the governments involved, federal and provincial, to look at the concerns of the industry.
Earlier this week I met with the coalition. On Wednesday I met with spouses of the truckers and yesterday I met with a delegation from the owner-operators now gathered in Ottawa.
My officials continue at this time to meet with these representatives to address the concerns which fall within federal jurisdiction. I have listened to and heard their concerns, and I understand them. I invited these truckers to join the task force process because this process is an appropriate forum for looking at this issue.
There have been a number of statements about the impact of federal policies on the industry. I would like to clarify some salient points.
First, free trade. The free trade agreement did not include any changes to the ground rules for the trucking industry. Second, under the old federal sales tax, while truckers did not pay sales tax on their purchases of tractors or trailers, they did pay federal sales tax on most other goods purchased, including fuel. The new GST effectively eliminates any federal sales tax from trucking inputs because the truckers will be refunded all the GST they pay on their rigs, fuel, parts, servicing and on other overhead.

Offsetting this preferential depreciation is the fact that the U.S. also levies a 12 per cent heavy truck and trailer excise tax which Canada does not.
Provincial fuel taxes tend to be higher than U.S. state taxes and this differential has been increased as a result of some provincial budgets, such as Ontario's and Quebec's, where fuel taxes were increased by 3.4 cents a litre over the period of the year 1991.

subtopic: ASSOCIATION OF POLISH ENGINEERS IN CANADA
ASSOCIATION OF POLISH ENGINEERS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Association of Polish Engineers in Canada, which is being celebrated this weekend in Ottawa. They are a shining example of all an NGO can be and can achieve.
In 1941, with only 100 engineers and a charter drafted by our own Senator George Mcllraith, then parliamentary secretary to C. D. Howe, they began the work of assisting professional newcomers to gain Canadian accreditation and technical language skills required for speaking and writing English.
By arranging for Canadian engineers to teach them, not only were the desired language skills learned, most students were hired by one of the Canadian companies that donated the teaching time.
With Sir Casimir Gzowski, an engineer and builder of our railroads and bridges, as their patron, they expanded to include chemists, physicists, and members of other related professions and now number in the thousands.
Today I ask all members of the House to join me in saluting the ingenuity, dedication and hard work which have resulted in this outstanding achievement by the Association of Polish Engineers in Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I had the opportunity to answer what was in effect that question yesterday when it was posed by the member for Saanich-Gulf Islands after my remarks in the House.
We have taken a decision that faced with the cynicism in Canada about elected officials we could either contribute to that cynicism by having parliamentarians walk away from our most basic responsibility for the future of the country, or we could try to change that cynicism by demonstrating that parliamentarians are effective and prepared in dealing with the nation's problems. But we are not going to do that in old ways. We are prepared to establish a joint committee of this House and the other place and then adopt the most original means we can to involve the Canadian public.
I said to her colleague in the House yesterday that I would very much welcome specific suggestions from the NDP, the Liberal Party, or indeed from individual members of the House, as to means by which we can preserve the well-established tradition of parliamentary democracy in this country and add to it the most effective possible involvement of other Canadians interested in this process.
As to actions speaking louder than words, I agree with her. That is why I began my responsibilities in this portfolio by acting, by going to talk directly to people who had felt excluded from the process in the past. I intend to continue to act in that way, as this government does.

Madam Speaker, it is clear that any constitutional decision will be made by the Parliament of Canada.
We will not be undermining the authority of the parliamentary tradition in Canada, it seems to me, if as politicians we show to Canadians that we are listening to what they have to say.
In fact, I am suggesting to the minister that that is our responsibility and our duty so that the process that we institute at the beginning indicates that we are listening to Canadians.
No one is suggesting that elected members would not be a part of that process. I am simply suggesting it should be enlarged to include those who are under-represented in this House.
I will say to the minister that women make up 51 per cent of the population of this country. They make up 14 per cent of the population of this House. Aboriginal people and visible minorities are under-represented in this House.
Will the minister consider seriously that we try a new way, perhaps a less traditional way, which will include elected officials but expand that process right from the beginning to show Canadians that we are listening and we are prepared to do something in a really new way?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the answer to that general question is yes.
Certainly I agree with the observation of the hon. member. It is one of the problems of any elected institution that it is not as representative of the country, demographically, as it should be.
Will we take a variety of means, as innovative as we can find, to listen to people, to involve them in the decisions? The answer to that is clearly yes. Will we abandon Parliament? The answer to that is no.
Our view is that Parliament needs to be reformed, but not abandoned. We recognize the cynicism that exists in the country. We think it is corrosive. We think that succumbing to that cynicism could in fact make it more difficult for us to build the kind of strong Canada we want. We intend to reform the way this Parliament works. We intend to reach out as widely as we can to
May 17, 1991

Oral Questions
involve Canadians in the process of deciding our future together, but we do not intend to abandon one of the institutions that has served this country very well in 124 years of our history.

Madam Speaker, no one is talking about abandoning Parliament. We are simply saying that this an extraordinary, absolutely serious and crucial issue for the future of Canada. Surely the authority of parliamentarians will be reinforced when we say that we are prepared to do things in an extraordinary, innovative way right from the beginning for this particular situation.
I think to characterize it as abandoning Parliament is clearly not presenting what I am suggesting.

I would remind the government that the Beaudoin-Edwards Committee will soon make its report public. Can the government promise today in this House that it will not ignore any recommendation to increase the participation of as many people as possible at the beginning of the process advocated by this report?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I clearly said yesterday in my speech in the House that I have no intention of judging the Beaudoin-Edwards committee report before it is received and I have no intention of rejecting the suggestions it may contain. If the Beaudoin-Edwards committee suggests ways for Parliament to consult Canadians better, I would be quite interested in hearing them and I intend to take them seriously.
As far as innovation is concerned, we already said in the Speech from the Throne the other day that, for the time in the history of our Parliament, we would give a parliamentary committee, as a formal part of its mandate, the right to work with elected provincial legislators and not only to consult them. That is something new. There are other ways to ensure more citizen participation, but on a parliamentary basis that serves Canada well.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Employment and Immigration I will direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister.
On Wednesday the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the only problem with the Al-Mashat case was not that Mr. Al-Mashat was admitted on the fast track, but that ministers did not know.
Once again the new Secretary of State for External Affairs has it all wrong. We will find out what ministers knew. We are equally concerned about why Al-Mashat was given a fast track when so many people are not given any preference, any kind of access, because they do not know people in high places.
I would like to ask the minister this question. In 1988, close to 27,000 Kurdish refugees escaped from the chemical attacks of the Iraqi government. Three thousand applied to come to Canada, and according to a report of the Turkish government, not one has been accepted or interviewed up to this time. They are still tragically waiting to be accepted.
Rather than being solely preoccupied with defending the reputation of ministers, when is this government going to afford the victims of the Iraqi government the same kind of treatment it gave to Al-Mashat.

The idea of a minister being responsible for everything that goes on in a department may once have been realistic, but it has long since ceased to be so. A minister cannot possibly know everything that is going on in a department. The doctrine of ministerial accountability undermines the potential for genuine accountability on the part of the person that ought to be accountable-the senior officer of the department.

Oral Questions
The recommendation, endorsed unanimously, was:
We recommend that all ministers co-operate with committees
exercising their expanded mandates by making available public
servants that may be called to testify before a committee.
We have made that commitment. That committee will implement these recommendations which were approved-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.

Madam Speaker, the problem with these ministers is not that they don't know everything that is happening in its departments, they don't know anything at all about what is going on in their departments. Especially when it goes into their own offices, they have no control or judgment on it.
If that minister is now speaking for government, my specific question is about why the Kurdish refugees who escaped from a brutal chemical attack are not given any consideration at all? I have a specific case of one of my own constituents who, over a year ago, married a Kurdish woman who has been sitting in Iran for close to a year without any kind of treatment or review whatsoever by the Department of Immigration.
Does this not show that there is an unfair and discriminatoiy system? I ask that minister, is that not one of the primary topics and subjects of investigation that the parliamentary committee must address: why the immigration system gives preference to people in high places but ignores the plight of ordinary citizens?

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there are no doubt cases where there is unfair and discriminatoiy queue jumping. I remember very well when one potential immigrant drove to Manitoba, was put into a ministerial car, given a ministerial driver and driven to Emerson, Manitoba for the Emerson shuffle so that he could be landed. Does the member remember that? We would be glad to bring that forward in the committee.

Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration and, in his absence, to the Acting Prime Minister.
Recently, Zbigniew Redka, a man of Polish origin, was told, after waiting for two years, he would have to wait another two years to have his immigration case heard. Shortly after, he hanged himself.
Last week, Jesus Saferino Aquilan, a Salvadoran refugee claimant committed suicide in Toronto.
How can the government of the day allow Mr. Al-Ma-shat, no friend of Canada, to jump the queue and yet have refugees and self-exiles wait three, four and five years for a landed immigrant status?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point I was trying to make by reading the McGrath committee report, which is the recommendation we have approved, is that these kinds of detailed questions are unsuitable, as this committee recommended, for this kind of exchange. They are good for scoring political points.
The committee will meet just as soon as his party co-operates with establishing the membership. In fact, those questions about Al-Mashat can be dealt with and we can put this strawman aside and deal with the real issues that affect Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I drew a potential suicide case from Montreal to the former minister of immigration's attention. Today the minister says: "People who are committing suicide because of the government's bungling should not be raised in this forum?"
I have just drawn attention to two cases. How many more such cases are there in the refugee backlog?
I would like to ask the minister if he will hold an inquest into the two cases that I have mentioned and report to Parliament? Will he agree today to grant work permits and permission to go to school to self-exiled refugees who have to wait 18 to 24 months for their landed immigrant status? Also, will he promise today in this House that the government will clear up all refugee backlog cases within six months?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity today to respond to the first question to come to me as the Minister of State for the Environment.
Hear, hear.

plan, in co-operation with the provincial governments and industry.
It was an opportunity for us to reach out to hear what people have to say and at the same time bring together the green plan of over some hundred initiatives.
Now we have an opportunity to bring forward the information about the green plan to the Canadian people. I am very pleased we are doing that and we are going to continue to be consulting and implementing the issues and the green plan.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the minister to her new position but my question is for the Acting Prime Minister about corruption and the need to do something about it.
I am sure it is just a coincidence, but would the Acting Prime Minister explain why Ian Anderson, the Prime Minister's former deputy communications director received $75,000 for communications advice on the green plan, or why Pat Delbridge who is now head of the government's environmental logo board received $200,000 for two months work last year?
Will the Acting Prime Minister support sending all of these contracts let so far under the green plan to a public auditing function by a special committee of this House to determine where these untendered $8 million are going and whether or not they are just going from the public purse to friends of the Conservative Party?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the green plan is a tremendous, major undertaking by the Canadian government and by the people of Canada. We want to discuss and implement these various initiatives which are set out in the green plan and we will continue to have these consultations and the implementation.
In relation to the particular issues that the hon. member has mentioned, there will a thorough analysis of all of this. The Minister of the Environment and myself are new to these positions. We are looking at all the analyses as to how we can communicate best with the people of Canada.

I would like to ask the Minister if he is aware that 39 women's clothing factories have closed down since 1986, resulting in some 2,000 lost jobs in the Montreal region and elsewhere in Quebec.

speechtext:

I can tell you that my predecessor was veiy, very effective and probably even more effective than my colleague opposite when he was Minister of Labour in Montreal.

Adjustment Program are negotiated with the provinces. It is a federal-provincial program.
We are now looking into the various regulations with the Quebec Minister, Mr. Bourbeau, and I can assure the Minister that we will do everything possible so that the workers in the Montreal region whom he has just mentioned can benefit from as many programs as possible offered by the Department of Labour and also the Department of Employment and Immigration.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for the Environment.
The minister, coming from metropolitan Toronto, is well aware of the fact that, like so many other Canadian cities, metropolitan Toronto is facing an imminent garbage crisis. One of the worst offenders in this crisis is excessive packaging.
Since the voluntary packaging program does not seem to be working, will the government introduce immediately a program of stiff regulations to reduce packaging and do it before the 1993 deadline or target date set in the green plan? If we do not do that, we are going to have garbage piled up in our back yards and our parks.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to first compliment the member for Don Valley East on his continued interest in environmental issues. I have worked with him on those in metro Toronto and I appreciate his good work.
The national protocol on packaging, as established by the environment ministers of Canada, is to reduce packaging by 50 per cent by the year 2000. Nobody in this House wants to wait till the year 2000 to have all of this done, so by 1993 we are going to have regulations. If by 1992 we see that the voluntary action, the consultation with the provinces, the consultation with industries, is not accomplishing what we want it to do, the federal government will put forward those regulations. The provinces monitor the volume of waste into the landfill sites so that will be our indication whether or not the program is working.

I want to say that the consumers themselves can do a great deal in terms of reducing waste. Just yesterday I received 30 letters from the-

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister for employment or the Minister of Labour. Yesterday Pascal's hardware, a successful Montreal business for 87 years, fell victim to the recession and went bankrupt. As a result 21 stores have closed and 1,600 employees have lost their jobs, many of them with more than 20 years service.
Would the minister say whether this massive lay-off will qualify for help under the program for older worker adjustment and what other initiatives does the government have to retrain and re-employ these workers?

With regard to the retraining, the hon. member is aware that the federal government through the Department of Employment and Immigration has a significant number of retraining programs. We could even have had more had the Official Opposition not blocked Bill C-21 for two years. We do have the programs in place and we will use them.

Madam Speaker, that is not enough. When is this government going to recognize it bears a heavy responsibility in closures such as this. The goods and services tax, high interest rates, the free trade agreement and mass crossborder shopping have all contributed to this closure.

Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, after two years of all-party activity on committee, there was unanimity among the parties to introduce Bill C-79 to regularize the relationship between the House and the RCMP in terms of responsibilities. There was unanimity in that regard.
When bills are given Royal Assent there is sometimes a time separation between Royal Assent and Proclamation, because administrative matters need to be taken care of and put in place. No such requirements were necessary with this bill.
When I became aware, as a result of a conversation with a member of Parliament whose offices were being searched by the RCMP at the time, that C-79 had not
been proclaimed, I was on my way out of town. Three days later when I got back, I asked my staff to have it proclaimed.
The reality is that it was given Royal Assent on April 11. It should have been proclaimed on April 12. It should have been passed last year.
The hon. member, in looking for conspiracy and in suggesting that there is something wrong in proclaiming a bill which was endorsed by both Houses, which was unanimously approved by all political parties in this House, is really, really searching for scandal. I wish he would be more sympathetic to peoples' reputations as members were sympathetic to his reputation when he had problems.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is rather interesting to note some of the comments of the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader who either intentionally or whatever brought these particular motions to the floor of the House today to seek unanimous consent of the House.
It was discussed earlier this morning with myself and the parliamentary secretary. There was a clear undertaking from the government that we would pursue discussions on these various matters. Obviously, in a sense of not wanting to co-operate with opposition members, they have proceeded to introduce these particular motions.
It should be noted that this is a very significant point of order, very, very significant. Since the beginning of this session contained in the throne speech, leading up to the throne speech and shortly thereafter, we have been hearing the buzz words and the rhetoric with regard to non-partisanship and co-operation among the parties.
We have co-operated when we have been consulted such as on the Beaudoin-Edwards committee. We have agreed to that. On the standing committee for health and welfare we have agreed to reinstate that. With regard to elections and privileges, we have been consulted on that and with regard to the references in terms of supply to the various standing committees, but lo and behold the government House leader is at it again. He is trying to drive things down our throats.
I am informing you, Madam Speaker, and through you members opposite, that members of this caucus and of this party are not going to put up with that. We are not going to accept that kind of conduct from government members opposite.
Very briefly my point of order will conclude. On the substance of those motions, the parliamentary secretary knows very well that the contents of those bills in many of those instances is that we have opposed them and opposed them vigorously. If they wish to proceed with them, they have an opportunity to lay the legislation before the House of Commons. But if they were so desirous of having all that legislation introduced, consummated and passed by Parliament, why did they not extend the sittings of the House and not call for a new Parliament?
The fact of the matter is that they do not want co-operation from opposition parties; they do not want that at all. They want to have it their way and to heck with those of us in the opposition.
I wish to inform you, sadly, Madam Speaker, that we in the opposition will not accept that kind of conduct from

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order to express to the House and to you, that I believe that an essential document for the functioning of our Parliament has not been provided for members of this House.
When the throne speech was presented to members of both Houses by His Excellency the Governor General, it was accompanied by a background paper which was provided to all members of the media. Members of the media, who were consulted only moments ago by myself and my colleagues, stated that they all received this document. No member of this House has received this document which accompanied the Throne Speech and which was entitled Background Paper. In other words, an explanatory note to the Throne Speech that was supposed to tell all of us how the document worked was given to members of the media and to no member on this side of the House, and it was probably not even given to the Chair.
It is essential that if this House is going to function, and if members are to be able to do their jobs, they must have access to all of those documents, a document which is supposed to be the original paper that tells us how the whole session is going to work.
Under the definition of privilege in Beauchesne's fifth edition citation 16 is stated:
Parliamentary privilege is the sum of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and by Members of each House individually, without which they could not discharge their functions and which exceed those possessed by other bodies or individuals.

May 17, 1991

If we cannot even get a copy of the totality of the throne speech of this Parliament, how can we as parliamentarians do our job?
There has been neglect on the part of the government, at the very least.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Probably even worse. I want to know, why in this House, you and I and other members of this House were not given a copy of the document, which is an explanatory document to the throne speech, at the same time that it was given to every single member of the media in this country.
The opposition House leader just indicated the lack of co-operation we are getting from the government. It is even worse when we cannot even get a copy of the throne speech.
Madam Speaker, I hope you and your officials will examine this situation because it goes to the very root of how this Parliament can or cannot function by the way this government is operating.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not believe that the hon. member has a case of privilege. I looked at the throne speech. I did not see anything in it that indicated an addendum or an annex that was attached to it, so I do not know what the hon. member was protesting about. If in fact the press received background briefings or press briefings, that is a normal practice that many of us engage in, including the hon. member who from time to time gives the press materials.
It is clearly not a question of privilege. It is clearly a matter of debate. I am sorry that the hon. member has chosen to use his Opposition Day to do that.

Madam Speaker, one of the principles on which Parliament operates is that Her Majesty the Queen is not to be injected into partisan debate. I regret very much that the deputy House leader for the government is taking this step. I hope that this will be noted in your ruling.
I want to draw your attention to a column which appeared in The Toronto Sun on May 15 written by Douglas Fisher. This column comments on the throne
speech. It speaks of the background paper which in the words of Mr. Fisher elaborates on the throne speech and which he calls "an accompanying paper".
Mr. Fisher goes on to quote the portion of the throne speech which says that the government will ask MPs to "consider new procedures for assessing legislation, for raising grievances on behalf of constituents and for questioning governments to further enhance the role of individual members and their greater independence". Then Mr. Fisher goes to say: "The background paper says much of the public debate about reform of Parliament is focused on free votes".
The background paper apparently also talks about the government's desire "to avoid what is visually and physically reinforcing the we and them phenomenon which largely dictates the outcome of votes."
This is not in the throne speech. This, according to Mr. Fisher, is in the background paper which, in the words of Mr. Fisher, elaborates on the throne speech. In other words, it gives information about the government's plans and intentions sketched out in the throne speech. Information which, if it pertains to the throne speech, should have been given to members no less than to the press.
It is clear from this column by Mr. Fisher, a longstanding commentator on Parliament and a former member of Parliament, that this background paper was more than just a press summary of the throne speech. It developed the government's ideas as set forth in the throne speech beyond the actual words of the throne speech. If that was the case, then the government had an obligation to present that background paper to Parliament in the same way, and frankly, at the very least, before it did so to the press.
Not having taken this step, if this is not a breach of the privileges of the House, certainly we have a valid point of order and I ask you to rule accordingly. By the way, I am sure that the assistant deputy House leader, the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, would want to make clear that if you find a prima facie case of privilege, one of us in the Official Opposition will be more than happy to move the appropriate motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to resume my speech in this important debate where it was interrupted at 11 o'clock this morning for the Business of the House.
So, Madam Speaker, as I was saying this morning, our government is aware of the truckers' situation. Let me repeat that we have already acted. Last year, we asked officials in my department to do a comprehensive study of the factors involved in cross-border competitiveness.
The study was divided into eight parts; the purposes of this study are to determine the nature and parameters of the Canadian share of the cross-border market, to evaluate the competitiveness of Canadian trucking companies in these markets and to analyze the impact of factors that can affect their ability to compete. The priority of all concerned is the comparative study of the Canadian and American tax systems. That is why we speeded up the process in that particular area.
The firm of Peat, Marwick, Thome has thus undertaken a thorough study of the tax systems in effect in both countries and their impact on the cross-border competitiveness of Canadian transportation. This study is to be printed this weekend, and I will then send it to task force members. Until then, it would be inappropriate for me to comment on the contents of the study, since the task force has not yet made it public.

Believe me, if I could I would because I believe it will, once and for all, lay to rest much of the negative misinformation that is currently being circulated about Canadian taxes.
May 17, 1991

The study has been extremely helpful in clarifying the issues. It shows, for example, that broad generalizations cannot be made about taxes and the trucking industry. There is not one over-all factor that explains disadvantages and advantages. Taxes obviously are not the only matter of concern to truckers.

For the other expenses concerning trends in crossborder transportation, analyses of the economic conditions for Canadian carriers operating in cross-border markets, a comparison of their economic performance, the costs of Canadian and American truckers in the cross-border market and an evaluation of alternative standards for cabotage, a study will cover and summarize all the action taken.
This study must be completed for the task force to review it and draw conclusions and make recommendations next week. All concerned must be present at the discussion table to be able to review this very important aspect of the studies. I am sure that every member of the task force will participate in this review and in making recommendations.
I would like to add a few words about the methodology of these studies. I am convinced that the way they were conducted can only give great credibility to their findings. So that no group in particular be targeted by any part of the studies, the task force was comprised of two groups of truck owners, one of them representing seven associations represented, as well as the three unions representing the majority of the transport companies employees, the Canadian Trucking Association, the Truckers Council which represents hundreds of truck fleet operations and six national freight associations.

As the provinces play a very prominent role in the administration of trucking regulations, each province and territory has a place on the task force.
Finally, because many federal departments are touched by the issues on the table, six federal departments are represented. No point of view was overlooked, as 40 different organizations are represented. Not all members attended every task force meeting but a good cross-section of each industry and government was
Supply
present at each one. They were present and actively participated in the selection of consultants. They have criticized the draft reports and sent the consultants back to do again various parts or all of the study in order to meet their demands. They are expected to meet for the sixth time on June 4 to criticize the wrap-up study and formulate their recommendations for action.
I fully expect that there will be work for everyone coming out of these recommendations, for the federal and provincial governments and for the industry itself. No one will get off scot-free. The task force has worked as a team. Even though some of its members have not always seen eye to eye, they have, in the vast majority of cases, gone away from meetings with a feeling of positive accomplishment.
I only wish that other jurisdictions were as co-operative on other issues as they have been with regard to the studies.

It is ironic that, just a few weeks ago, the Premier of Ontario wrote the Ontario Truckers Association to tell them, and I quote: "Having worked closely with Ed Philip, the Ontario Minister of Transport, you are certainly aware that we are presently reviewing the short term tax measures affecting the trucking industry."
I bet the Ontario Trucking Association was surprised when it found out that the real intentions of the government had to do with tax measures concerning the trucking industry. Over the past few days, many figures were quoted concerning the number of bankruptcies in the trucking industry in accounts from truckers, from the media and from the members opposite.
While there is a proportional increase in the percentage of bankruptcies in this industry, it does not exceed what can be expected in such a cyclical industry as trucking.
I know that this is of little comfort to those affected, but the number of bankruptcies in the US trucking industry also reached a record high in 1990.
Some claim also that the American carriers are taking all the work away from Canadian companies. It may seem like that because the figures from Statistics Canada indicate that tonnage carried by trucks between Canada

May 17, 1991
Supply
and the United States dropped 7 per cent between 1988 and 1989, and declined an additional 3 per cent last year.
Before 1988, Madam Speaker, Canadians had an apparent advantage because of the deregulation of the trucking industry in the United States in 1980. It is a fact that since January 1, 1988, there are more U.S. carriers in Canada. This, combined with a drop in traffic as a result of the recession, accounts for the difference in market share, compared with what the situation was like before.
I would like to focus a few moments on the impact of the recession. We can give many reasons why the present recession hurts as much as it does. One is that we had previously enjoyed a period of unprecedented strong economic growth.
Entry controls in the trucking industry were relaxed in the early 80s, soon after U.S. deregulation. During the five years prior to January 1,1988,95 per cent of trucking licences were issued by provincial transport commissions.
Many new Canadian companies started operations during this period, and we have good reason to believe that many will survive to enjoy the next period of growth which all economists say will start in a matter of weeks. These companies are challenging old concepts and bringing innovative solutions to the industry. We need these companies to become competitive on new world markets.
Our truckers would never have acquired the requisite "lean and mean" approach if we had continued to hide them behind the protective walls of regulation. We have good reason to believe the economy will recover in the fall. Our truckers will be ready to respond to this economic renewal and to the higher wages the Free Trade Agreement will bring as a result.
Meanwhile, I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that I and my colleagues on this side of the House have listened to the genuine demands made by the hardworking and determined men and women in the trucking industry. We are actively trying to find ways to help them weather the present storm. We have asked all parties, including governments, labour, the trucking industry and the business community to co-operate with us. I am convinced, Madam Speaker, that in the course of the process that is now going on, which includes all parties involved in this area, we will find the kind of solutions
that will help these men and women who are truck owners and who represent a very substantial part of the vitality of Canada's trucking industry.

Madam Speaker, I listened to the minister attentively. I would like to ask him a couple of questions.
He referred to the fact that as minister he is not able to refer to some of the findings of the studies that have been commissioned by this government. I am wondering how he reconciles that comment with that of his predecessor who, in a letter to the Canadian Trucking Association, said quite clearly that he would not be prepared to wait until the final chapter is written on those studies, and that he would like to commence on some of the obvious findings rather than waiting.
It seems that the comments of today's minister are very much at odds with those of his predecessor.
Second, I am wondering if he could perhaps explain what he meant in today's Toronto Star where he is quoted as saying that there is "one major component" of the cost of doing business as a trucker in Canada that can make our drivers uncompetitive with American drivers. He has suggested that there is one trump card in a deck of options that he has focused on. I am wondering whether he can clarify for this House and for Canadians what that one major piece of the puzzle is.
Last, could he inform us or provide us with an update-again, I made reference to the fact that I thanked him for meeting with the delegation. He has been meeting for over a day. The meetings are still ongoing. Could he give us an update as to how the discussions are going. Are there any specific items on the table that he can tell us about and any commitments that have been made to show that there is indeed momentum and not just meetings? Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in reply to the first question, I think that what I said earlier contradicts in no way what my predecessor wrote in his letter because, aside from these studies, work that could be conducted in-house, within the Department, was indeed undertaken. May 17, 1991

Department, whether we will be able to answer this or that question and, more importantly, discuss the facts.
As regards the status of the present round of discussions, I have no indication that they are over. So, I have to assume they are ongoing. The meeting started yesterday afternoon, at 5:30 p.m., and went late into the evening. Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the minister about some remarks he made before the Question Period started in which he said that the Canadian Trucking Association refused to co-operate in drafting a code of ethics for truckers. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will certainly not get into a debate here on what someone might or might not have said. The information I obtained from throughout my department indicates that what I said just now is accurate. Madam Speaker, I had asked a second question of the minister. I am wondering if he went on honestly to the last question. I appreciate that if an agreement was made with the truckers not to release detail it is something that the minister and the truckers will have to honour.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:

After we did so, we mutually agreed to extend the talks last night.
