May 17, 1991
Supply

Madam Speaker, I could not agree more with the vice-president, who says that the government is hiding behind studies.
I would like to ask the minister what his department has been doing for the last three years. Presumably, before the department embarked on the deregulation of the industry, which was a precursor to the free trade agreement, there should have been some studies done.
In the same way as the Department of Finance kept most of those studies secret from the public, I believe that there were studies done in his department as to what the effect of deregulation would be and what the specific effect of the government's tax policies will be. If studies were not done then clearly the government moved in a manner which showed complete and utter disregard for the jobs of Canadians.
The minister said that he is waiting until the studies come in. His predecessor said he did not have to wait for the studies to come in. I would like to ask him specifically what action he is prepared to announce today in the House of Commons to give some hope to those truckers and their families who will remain here on the Hill. The tie-ups across the province of Ontario have had an effect on its already reeling economy. Is the minister going to continue to allow that to happen and is he going to continue to play political Ping-Pong with his friend Premier Rae of Ontario who, like the minister, is not prepared to hit this problem head on and provide some real solutions to the truckers?
[ Translation ]

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the hon. member for Hamilton East makes statements like the one she just made, she does not lead us all to practical solutions. As I said in this House several times, it is precisely to determine whether the perceptions and allegations of the Canadian tax system putting owner operators at a disadvantage are accurate or not. The government did not decide to conduct studies-I repeat it and I will go on repeating it forever-it was the various interested parties. The provincial governments, in spite of what our friends opposite
might say, have a tremondous responsibility in this issue because of the taxes they impose on diesel fuel.
It is therefore at the request of the interested parties that we created this task force made up of all interested groups and this task force decided to conduct studies to establish the facts.

I would like to tell my hon. colleague that in the end there are many people who are saying that deregulation has not been detrimental to the trucking industry, and that in fact is has had significant positive benefits to the whole trucking sector.

Madam Speaker, I want to first say to my colleague from York West that I am very pleased that he and his party moved this motion today, and I want to compliment him on his speech because it is about the same as I would have said. I probably could endorse 90 per cent of the remarks he made.
When we get into these kinds of crises, we all forget some essential things about transportation. Without a good, efficient, functioning transportation system, all modes that operate at a reasonable profit and the entire economy of the country grind to a halt. Transportation is the foundation of any economy of any country.
Successive governments have played fast and loose with transportation policy in the name of so-called free enterprise, competition, competitiveness and so forth. Today it is not just the trucking industry that is hurting and is in real trouble, but the railroads as well. There are essentially only two of those. Why? Because of the very thing that the minister just said, that deregulation helped them, when the opposite is the case.
I do not know if the minister was here when I sat on the standing committee when we dealt with the government white paper on deregulation for over two years. We held hearings all across the country. Repeatedly, we were promised by the government that something would be done about many things, including the differences in the tax laws between Canada and the United States.
When we were dealing with the legislation in 1987, which took effect in January 1988, we were promised that with deregulation something would be done about a number of matters and still all we are having are studies.
May 17, 1991

Supply
I keep hearing about the word "competitiveness". The word "competitiveness" has been in the government's vocabulary ad nauseam for a long time. "A level playing field", that is another one.
By the very laws, rules and regulations that the federal government and all 10 provinces are carrying out, they are hurting the competitive capacity of the trucking and railway industries in Canada. They are at a disadvantage with the United States operators. Last year in the province of Ontario alone, 675 trucking firms went bankrupt. That is as a direct result of deregulation.
Everybody wants into the act and all that happens is they take turns going broke. When they go broke because of laws and regulations, or lack of laws and regulations, by the federal government, it means the federal government itself is to blame for any lack of competitiveness in the trucking industry in the railroads.
Then there is this level playing field. If you walk out on a baseball diamond or on a football field, you will see that they are not level. They are sloped. They are higher in the middle than on the sides and the ends.
This level playing field that the government has devised under the free trade agreement and deregulation is sloped. It is sloped all down hill to the U.S.A. What the hell is the use of having a level playing field if according to our own laws, rules and regulations, or lack of, the other guy has the ball on our 10-yard line all the time? We have to start from behind. It does not matter whether it is the trucking industry, and it is not just peculiar to Ontario and Quebec. It is the case in every province across Canada.
American railroads can do things in Canada that Canadian railroads cannot do in the United States, depending on what state they are in. That part of the playing field has never been made level. That is part of deregulation and the free trade agreement.
The tax laws have been gone into, the depreciation schedules. I will not repeat what my friend from York West had to say, but let me remind the Chair that the submission to the federal minister's task force by the Canadian Trucking Association recommended that: "In the case of the depreciation rate issue, the Canadian Trucking Association urges the Government of Canada to take immediate actions to equalize the depreciation schedules for tractors and trailers in Canada with those in the United States. It is anticipated that by undertaking this action approximately 20 per cent of the current
competitive disadvantage experienced by the Canadian based motor carriers would be eliminated".
That should also apply to the Canadian railroads, which are victimized by the same kind of depreciation schedule for their rolling stock as our trucking industry is.
In the case of truck tractors, in the United States a tractor owner can write off one-third of it in the first year; in Canada it is 15 per cent. In the second year he can write off another 45 per cent of it; in Canada, 25 per cent. By the fourth year the American carrier can write off the remaining 7 per cent; in the thirteenth year the Canadian carrier can write off the last .5 per cent.
It is similar in the case of trailers: 20 per cent depreciation for a U.S. carrier in the first year, 15 per cent for Canadian; 32 per cent for an American carrier in the second year, 25 per cent for Canadian, and so on down through the piece.
I do not understand the stubbornness. This matter of depreciation schedules was also raised with the previous Liberal government and we got nowhere.
I have been through 14 ministers of transport since I came here in 1968. They should have a revolving door in the minister's office. Every damn one of them, Liberal or Tory, it did not make any difference, would not act.
There is another matter about fuel taxes. All the provinces have a fuel tax and the federal government has a fuel tax. In the United States, fuel taxes are earmarked; 97 per cent of its fuel taxes go into highway infrastructure of all kinds and 7 per cent into mass transit. In Canada, the federal government which collects something in the order of $600 million, puts 5 per cent, is for mainly the Trans-Canada Highway through national parks and nothing else. The government threw out the entire revolving fund for grade separations. Rail line relocation has disappeared.
If the federal government would at least use the fuel taxes it collects to finish four-laning the Trans-Canada Highway, northern Ontario alone would be a $2 billion to $3 billion tab. In the western provinces we are looking at another $1 billion. When we drive through northern Ontario heading west, any resemblance between that and the Trans-Canada Highway is laughable. They could at least spend the fuel taxes on transportation but, no, it

May 17, 1991
Supply
goes into general revenue and the government can do whatever it likes with it.
The finance department does not like dedicated taxes. There are some that should be dedicated or earmarked and the fuel tax is one of them. It is a user fee and you use those taxes for the infrastructure-roads, bridges, highways, and grade separations or whatever-as the Americans do. I am not all that complimentary about very much in the United States, but that is one thing it uses some good sense on. We cannot get it here. Since you are not going to use those fuel taxes for transportation then why not reduce them? Otherwise you are collecting taxes under false pretences. It is a transportation user tax and it is not being used on transportation.
There is another matter that I have raised in this House repeatedly since the mid-1970s, in the days of the late unlamented Otto Lang, figuratively speaking.
He was Liberal, was he not?
Oh, yes. What is the difference?
Or even the good party.

Yes. They are the good guys now, you see. If they had done all the things they said today back when they were in power, there would not be a Tory government in place. But that is all right.
The whole matter of interprovincial and international trucking or any kind of interprovincial-intemational transportation, under our Constitution, comes under federal jurisdiction. There are no ifs, ands or buts about it.
In the late 1950s and early 1960s, the federal government of that day transferred the administration and the responsibility for that over to the provinces. Ever since then we have had a jungle. We have had 13 jurisdictions: 2 territories, 10 provinces and the federal government, running in 13 directions. It does not matter whether it is load limits, speed limits, size of trucks or safety standards, the jungle is still there. That is something else that we were repeatedly promised. In the two years we spent on the white paper on deregulation and in the almost one year we spent on the bill itself, we were repeatedly told by the government and the then Ministers of Transport that meetings were going on.
I think it was three different Tory Ministers of Transport who came before the transport committee with their annual estimates and a statement and assured us, time after time, of how they were negotiating with the provinces to arrive at a standard that applies across the country.
We have still got some more studies. After all these years, where is this standard? The federal government, through an Order in Council or whatever it takes, has the constitutional jurisdiction to say to the provinces: "We are setting the standards. If you will not agree among yourselves, if you will not negotiate the common standards across the country, then we will do it for you because we have the constitutional authority".
I am sick and tired of various provincial governments in their parochial little centres, and that is of all parties, that do not consider the whole country. We are the ones who have to consider the whole country. If we do not, who the hell is going to? I am tired of these baronial premiers who worry only about their own little bailiwick and not about their fellow Canadians.
There is another area. My colleague from York West mentioned that as well. I liked pretty well all of his nine points. In general, I can support them and I am sure my colleagues will.
I had discussions with Canadian Trucking Association representatives a year ago in which they told me that five or six medium and large Canadian trucking companies had just picked up their head offices and their operations and moved across the border. It is still going on and it is going to get worse. We will end up without a Canadian trucking industry worthy of the name.
The problem is deregulation. If you can find a bank manager to lend you the money, lease a second-hand tractor and, if necessary, a second-hand trailer, you can automatically get a licence and go into business the next day.
The established trucker who has his own mechanics, maintenance and everything else and has put 20, 30 or 40 years into his business has to compete with that. That is one of the results of deregulation. It threw the industry
May 17, 1991

into a jungle. It is survival of the fittest. That applies to Mother Nature, but deregulation is not our mother and it is not natural, nor is it fit.
In a society supposedly trying to keep this country together from east to west and from the 49th parallel to the Arctic, all the government does is to continue to divide us. All it does is allow this kind of squabbling to go on without having the courage to take some decisive actions.
Tommy Douglas taught me that I would rather lose for doing something than win for doing nothing. When the devil are you going to take action to re-regulate.
I am glad to note that Ontario has placed a two year moratorium on new licences in the trucking industry. I hope all the provinces do that. It is overdue. We need more trucking companies like we need a hole in the head.
I want to say to the hon. member for York West that we appreciate the motion he moved. In general, we liked the contents of his speech and I hope the government will decide as a result of today's debate that there are some actions they can and should take.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague who just spoke probably stopped his watch 90 years ago. He is talking to us about the socialist rhetoric that has failed most of the countries in the world that have implemented it. The only countries in the world that are successfully governed by socialists are succeeding because they have returned to the free market and the laws of the free market.
The hon. member said that deregulation has caused all these problems. He asked a question, but I have still not decided in my mind what competitiveness means.
I would like to say to the hon. member that competitiveness-
I do not remember that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Maybe he does not remember from one minute to the next what he said. That is precisely what he said.
Supply
The capacity to compete with others is very closely tied to deregulation. Regulation prevents players in any given field from having the flexibility necessary to meet the competition from other countries.
I would like to show hon. member through a little bit of arithmetic. He talked about the federal excise tax which, as I said this morning and I will repeat it again, is 4 cents a litre. The federal excise tax in the U.S. is 6.2 cents. The federal excise tax on fuel in the U.S. is almost 60 per cent higher than in Canada, per litre. In the U.S., it is 6.2 cents and ours is 4 cents.
The hon. member also wants to ignore the fact that the provincial sales tax on fuel is the crippling aspect of the situation. The fuel tax in Michigan, with which most Ontario truckers compete, is 4.6 cents per litre.
By the end of this year, when the announced increases are implemented by his friend from the branch in Toronto, it will be 14.3 cents. He complains about the federal excise tax and the taxing system which is 60 per cent or at least 40 per cent less in Canada than in the U.S.
At the same time he does not see much wrong with the fact that the government with which he is friends is imposing a provincial fuel tax that is 300 per cent of the one that is implemented by the corresponding U.S. state.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad we got another 10-minute speech out of the minister.
I was complaining about all the sales and excise taxes but at least the provinces, all of them, spend as much as they collect from fuel taxes, or more, on highways, roads, streets, sidewalks and mass transit. They do not specifically earmark it, but that is where the money is spent.
The federal government's contribution to the transportation infrastructure in this country is abysmal. If the government is not going to use the tax it is collecting for transportation then it should get rid of it.
My point was that despite all this talk from the government and in the throne speech about competitiveness it cannot happen because the laws we have, whether they are deregulation or provincial and federal taxes, prohibit Canadian trucking and railway industries from really competing.

Supply
Unless those laws are changed, the deck is stacked against them. The government has allowed the other side, the Americans, to have the ball on our 10-yard line all the time in a so-called level playing field. That is not fair ball.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by commending my hon. friend on his very fine, articulate, and at times very passionate speech in defence of some national responsibilities that ought to be discharged somewhat more forcefully.
The minister compared fuel taxes between the United States and Canada. It says in my statistics-perhaps we can take another look at it-that the American federal tax is 4.6 cents a litre whereas ours is 4.0 cents a litre.
Theirs is in fact slightly higher. However, what the minister failed to mention is that the base price for diesel fuel in the United States is 18.6 cents a litre compared to 37.9 cents a litre in Canada.
Therefore, while the two excise taxes charged by the two national governments are almost the same, the big differential is in the spread between the base prices. That is why I believe we on this side have been making an argument that we need to obviously be very concerned with both the federal and provincial excise taxes simply because the base prices are veiy, very different.
I am wondering if the hon. member can perhaps make a comment on that debate and, second, if he would be able to offer his analysis and his party's views on the fact that the government seems so intent on issuing study after study after the advent of deregulation, when in fact those studies ought to have properly been done before the deregulation door was swung open. I am wondering what his rationale would be for a government which studies the down effects after a policy has been undertaken, as opposed to having it done in the reverse order.

The hon. gentleman is quite correct about his analysis and the statistics he has. I might add that slightly less than 40 cents per litre, depending on the volume purchased, is the diesel fuel cost in Ontario. The cost of diesel fuel on the more concentrated U.S. trucking routes is 26 cents.
I heard on CBC Radio news this morning of 33 cents cost in upper New York State compared to 53 cents in Canada, and 56 cents on gasoline.
That kind of handicap destroys any possibility for competitiveness. Surely that requires both the federal and provincial governments acting in concert, and not more studies. We have had studies up to our ears.
I remember the two years we spent on the white paper, and we heard witnesses from Halifax to Victoria. Then-big corporations wanted deregulation, but we did not hear that very much from the transportation industry.
I want to say that the whole ideological binge that the government is on has got to stop. Their policies have proven to be harmful, are hurting this country, hurting its sovereignty, hurting its independence, and hurting a hell of a lot of people in this country.

speechtext: Very well. Back to the debate. The hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you probably noticed, like I did, that this was not a point of order.
May 17, 1991

I am glad to be able to take part in this debate today, and I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for York West, for presenting this motion to the House.

Canada's trucking industry is a $12 billion business. It employs directly and indirectly almost half a million Canadians. It is indeed big business and it is a business that we should all strive to help, to assist and hope to conserve, both for the near and distant future.
A little more than a year ago the government was made aware of the difficulties of this industry, if it did not know even before then through the blockages that occurred at a number of border points.

At that time, Mr. Speaker, the government was already aware of the problems. In fact, in 1988, the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel and I made speeches in the House against the deregulation bill, the bill tabled by the government opposite to deregulate the transportation industry.
We said at the time that the rules were not the same on both sides of the border and that deregulation would immediately give U.S. truckers an advantage. Perhaps the minister would care to check Hansard to see what opposition members said. Unfortunately, all of this proved to be true. I say unfortunately, because a lot of my constituents are hurting now.

On April 26 of this year a number of my colleagues and I were holding task force hearings on the deindustrialization of our country. In Alexandria, Ontario, we met with a number of truckers who came to tell us the state the trucking industry was in.
Three days later, on April 29,1 sent an open letter to the Minister of Transport and had it hand delivered to his office here on Parliament Hill. To this date the letter remains unanswered, not even an acknowledgement has yet been received by my office. In that letter I outlined for the minister the problems that were related to us by Mrs. Janet Keusch who was here a few days ago and met with the minister.
Supply
They told us very clearly the troubles the industry was in. They told us that not only was Glengarry Transport, GTL, having big problems but so were they, the small truckers, the truckers, the brokers, and the independent operators of the difficulties.
They told us about the depreciation rules that they felt were unfair. They told us about the fuel that was considerably more expensive in Canada-I am reading from the letter that I sent to the minister-insurances which are very high, the unreasonably high deductibles that they have to deal with on insurance, and of course they told us about the border problems where U.S. truckers come here with little or no verification as to the safety of their vehicles.
Most of all they talked to us about the GST which stands for, they say, "government squashes truckers''. The GST, the minister tells us, is reimbursed to the truckers for their fuel and input costs. When? I have yet to find a trucker who has received a GST cheque. Today is May 17. The GST has been in effect since January 1.

Since January 1, the truckers in my riding and across Canada lend this government money every time they pay the GST. They file for their refund but they never get the money, Mr. Speaker. To justify its position, the government says: They will get interest on their refund. Mr. Speaker, when his company is bankrupt, receiving $3 or $10 in interest is no help to a trucker who just lost his business, his home and all his assets. That is something the government should understand.

Now the government tells us it has seven studies which were started a year ago. Why does it take this long to have studies done? Why can we not get at least interim relief for the truckers? And why has that not been contemplated before now? This is a little hard to understand.
The Minister of Transport will know of the letter sent by his predecessor, the member for Simcoe North, in which he said earlier this year that he would not wait for the outcome of the studies. I quote from the letter of January 11,1991, which was sent to Mr. A. K. Maclaren.
It says:

May 17, 1991
Supply
I have no intention, however, of waiting until all the studies are
complete, to take any action which becomes evidently necessary-
The highways are blocked with truckers. Is it not evidently necessary that something has to be done? Glengarry Transport, Canada's fourth largest trucking company, has gone bankrupt and 1,800 people have lost their jobs. Is it not evidently necessary that something has to be done?
According to a May 9 story in The Financial Post Kingsway Transport is for sale, Federal Industries wants to get rid of it because they are not making any money with the company. Is it not evidently necessary that something has to be done?
The letter of April 29 that I sent to the minister remains unanswered. Three times I tried on behalf of my constituents to get a meeting with the minister, for Glengarry Transport. Once I managed to get a call back from one of his assistants. The meeting was never held between that minister and Glengarry Transport.
The closest I managed to get to the minister was in the lobby with three women, one of whom was from my riding. The minister, in his condescending way, refused to let me be there with my constituents. To make it worse, he did not want to appear outside the House of Commons within the same television screen in case there were cameras there with the MP representing the people in question. That is the kind of work that was done by that minister across the way, and I point the finger at him.
In the moment or two that I have left, I must say, though, at the very least his seat mate, the Associate Minister of Transport, did agree to meet with the people of GTL. She did try. I know it was at the last minute. We were only 24 hours away from the bankruptcy, but when I failed to get a meeting with the senior Minister of Transport, at least I managed to get one with the Minister of State for Transport, who at least was willing to hear the concerns of my constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the Minister of Transport-I realize he may be a little newer at this game than some of us-that it is high time he helped the industry and my constituents, 1,800 people in Canada in the case of Glengarry, and the 656 other companies that went
bankrupt last year and all other Canadians who lost their jobs.
In a letter dated January 11, the minister's predecessor told us he would not wait for the results of the studies. If that is still the government's policy, I would like to know now whether the government intends at least to take certain measures to help trucking companies, before it announces further measures later on.

Finally, to the people sitting at our left, they should remember the last increase in the price of diesel fuel by the the Government of Ontario. While both the federal government and the Government of Ontario are arguing with each other, trying to figure out which of the two is the worst culprit, my constituents are going bankrupt. The people of my riding do not have jobs. People elsewhere in Canada in the trucking industry need help.

So I want to ask the minister today, in this very last minute, this last hour which may be crucial for many truckers, to help them by at least announcing a number of measures.
I know he had several meetings with the truckers during the past few days, and I hope we will get at least a few measures that will give hope to the people who are about to lose everything, everything-excuse the repetition-as a result of this government's deregulation policy which was introduced in 1988.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue on the same theme as my colleague, the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I would also like to let him know my concerns and that I too understand the truckers, as I just said to his colleague from York West.
These people have problems, Mr. Speaker. They did long before the GST, long befere deregulation, maybe even before some of my colleagues came to this place, except for the hon. member who just spoke. He has been here for at least 25 years. As I was saying, these people do have problems, not only fuel and tax problems, but
May 17, 1991

also major problems with insurance, licences, buying trucks and repairs.
I can remember garage owners I was dealing with telling me 15 years ago: "Truckers are all fine people. They are having a rough time, but we cannot fix their trucks if they cannot pay the bill." I can tell you that, 15 years ago, many of my colleagues had never heard of the GST stood for. I can see that the opposition always comes up with the same suggestion: "Tike a step forward, a step backward, a step forward. Remove the GST; that will solve the problem."
Even if we removed all taxes-GST and federal tax-tomorrow morning, these guys would not go a block that they would face the same problem. They would come back and say: "Mister Minister, we are still experiencing problems." The minister mentioned that the report is about to be released. I hope so. The truckers are not looking for a quick fix or a two bit solution. They want a long term solution to their problem. Were licences issued? I remember the provinces used to make the decisions and issue licences. I went to get one myself at the Quebec Transport Commission. So, they made the decisions. Unfortunately, they made the wrong decisions at some point because there were too many requests. We cannot prevent people from earning a living, but regulations may be needed in certain circumstances.
The "forward, backward" solution the Liberals are suggesting is not to remove the GST, for the truckers do not pay GST or, if they do, they can get a refund.
They never got it!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They never got it. Did they ask for a it? My colleague mentioned that GTL Transport just went bankrupt. I would like to point out to him that there was no GST in 1990. What would the ideal solution be in his view? Would it be to remove the GST or to keep the truckers safely protected by regulation?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russel has the floor for two minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first the hon. member opposite just told us that the industry had problems before 1988. First, in the case of Glengarry Transport, that is not true. The company was founded in 1948. For 40 consecutive years,
Supply
GTL made profits, from 1948 to 1988. In 1988, the company started to incur losses and this has continued until 1991. That means, since deregulation. I want to tell the hon. member opposite, Mr. Speaker, that at last report, GTL was losing a million dollars a month. This is a company that made profits until 1988 and that had always been profitable.
The hon. member opposite asks us what we Liberals propose to do. I thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity to read once more the proposals of my colleague, the hon. member for York West-

The hon. member for York West proposed earlier today-I will repeat it for the benefit of my colleague across the way-quicker write-off provisions, federal excise tax relief on diesel fuel, more fairness for the GST on billing.
He wants to have a better system for the GST rebate on fuel, deduction of licence expenses, meetings of federal and provincial transport ministers to solve longterm problems and federal-provincial trade-off issues, stricter enforcement and higher penalties for American firms engaging in cabotage and a temporary moratorium on new interprovincial licences.
I thank my colleague for asking those questions again. They were all answered about an hour ago, but it gives us another chance to put them on the record.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity today to speak on a very important industry to the province of Ontario and to Canada.
As the truckers outside this Parliament park their rigs, they wait for action from this government.
If I may, on behalf of the truckers, Dale Hellier, Diane Bell, Dave Wallace and many more offer their thanks to the OPP, the RCMP and the security officers for the courtesy that has been shown to them while they have been here in Ottawa on the Hill. It has been greatly appreciated.
Driving a truck is more than a job, it is a way of life and the current federal government is destroying that dream for many. I have been a truck driver travelling all over the prairies. I know the intense feeling of independence,

May 17, 1991
Supply
of getting the job done on time and with a great deal of pride.
I drove auto transport to Saskatchewan, through small towns in Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Manitoba. I also drove in the sugar beet industry and drove the grain runs in southwestern Ontario for many years.
The trucking industry is crucially important to Ontario. It is the lifeblood of every community, especially in the smaller and rural areas. Virtually every person in the province, whether they realize it or not, depends on trucks to keep the products we all use and consume every day moving and available.
Trucks move every product and commodity: consumer goods like appliances and furniture; bulk commodities like grain and fertilizer; delicate products such as fresh fruit, meat and vegetables; major products such as cars, steel, livestock and heavy machinery; and the most intricate products such as scientific instruments and computers. They serve every Ontario community accessible by road, and every day, in some way, they contribute to the lives of every person in Ontario and Canada.
Think of the human factor. Hospitals, food and grocery stores, drug stores and gas stations cannot operate without direct transportation. Indeed, in Ontario, truck transportation accounts for nearly 70 per cent of the total freight shipped. Trucks generate more gross income than all other modes of transportation combined, estimated to be $24 billion just five years ago.
The industry employs over 250,000 people in Ontario; they are drivers, mechanics, computer specialists, marketing experts, terminal workers, accountants and administrators. In fact, the trucking industry employs fully five per cent of the provincial labour force. As well, the Ontario trucking industry, responsible for nearly half of all the trucking activity in Canada, spends over $5 billion in operating expenses.
In addition, it is worthy to note that every sector of the economy relies to some degree on trucking services. As a result, trucking activities have higher than average multipliers or spin-off effects in Ontario. So if the federal government, at this time, would let them have a rebate
they would receive the money back many times over with men being employed and able to operate.
A recent study by Coopers and Lybrand said that a one dollar increase in trucking activity generates more than two dollars worth of goods and services in other sectors. So the money the government does not receive today by allowing them a few breaks will come back manyfold. When the trucking industry is hurting we are all hurting.
Trucking firms paid the federal government more than $70 million in federal corporate income tax. Ontario motor carriers paid over $170 million in federal excise taxes on the diesel fuel they consumed. The little bit of taxes on the fuel saved now could keep these people working and more money in circulation. Of course, none of that money will help to rebuild the road and highway system, so important to truckers and an efficient economy.
I hope that sets in everyone's mind just how important a profitable trucking industry is to Canada and especially Ontario.
I met with many truckers outside on Wednesday. I speak their language. There were no bureaucrats or cabinet ministers or studies or task forces or committees or politics. We spoke straight up with no bull. These people are hurting. Their pride is being devastated. One of the drivers from Windsor, a 21 year veteran, said he could not help but break down and ciy. His frustration was very evident; he has lost his truck, his home and his family.
These truckers, the independent and free spirits of the open road, are having their dreams shattered by deregulation and the big American firms. All they want is a level playing field. Then watch us compete.
A trucker from Ridgetown in my riding was laid off just last month by Central Transport, a division of McKinlay. Two years ago there were 240 drivers; today there are just 67 left, as the routes are being gobbled up by the Americans, with little or no reaction from the federal government. That is just one example of many, many hundreds in my own riding who have lost their trucks and their jobs.
It has been brought to my attention that the American trucks are engaging in cabotage, something that is
May 17, 1991

supposedly illegal. Americans are dropping off loads from General Motors in Oshawa, and then taking another load from there to London or Hamilton. They are only supposed to be allowed one drop, one hook.
I would like to know from the government how many American trucks have been inspected and verified at weigh scales to prevent cabotage. Truckers tell me that because of government cutbacks the number of inspectors has been reduced. Since deregulation, how many additional inspectors have been hired by Transport Canada to enforce our rules? How many charges have been laid?
The truckers' concerns are well know, and my colleague from York West has outlined them extremely well. It was nearly one year ago that truckers were forced to block border points to get the attention of this government. The issues are still the same. But the only response over a year has been the creation of studies. Meanwhile, small and independent truckers are going under every day, losing their trucks, their homes, their families and their dignity.
Because deregulation has relaxed or eliminated government regulation of routes and tariffs, it has opened the door for more competitors, bringing predatory rates.
Because Canadians pay higher taxes and fuel costs, deregulation has left them vulnerable to low-cost Americans. Since 1986, the Ontario trucking industry has lost over 6,000 jobs to the U.S. through no fault of our truckers. It costs about 20 per cent more to send a shipment in a Canadian truck than an American one. With deregulation our firms are left wide open for bankruptcy. Depreciation rates for Canadian trucks are based on 13 years instead of four as in the United States. There is no level playing field on the trans-border issue.
The former Minister of Transport met truckers last year at the Windsor border crossing. He listened. He even sent out a news release that said he will act on the grievances of Canadian truckers. But this is government by task force, action through shuffling paper and bureaucrats and no results. So we have truckers and their families parked outside Parliament Hill and blocking major highways in Ontario.
Why does it take that sort of protest to get the attention of this government? Why does this government not listen? We have native blockades at Oka, people protesting CBC cutbacks, slashes to VIA Rail, army base
Supply
closures. The list goes on. This government, I am afraid, is destroying people's way of life through their policies, a plan to tear Canada apart.
The Ontario trucking industry must be saved from oblivion. Since 1988, the year of deregulation, no trucking firm has been in the black. I do not follow the government's logic, that to be competitive with the Americans, we tilt the playing field in their favour and throw our truckers to the wolves. We just make it impossible for people to compete.
It must also be mentioned that the Ontario socialist government has a role to play here. The NDP's recent budget was practically the straw that broke the camel's back.
A huge increase in the diesel fuel tax, $15 more tax for every fill-up; $4,000 more every year just in taxes. That is the socialist solution to our trucking woes, while the Tories in this House seem to ignore the real problems and set up task forces that are covered with a years' worth of dust.
Trucking is essential to Ontario and to Canada, especially as we try to meet the challenges of the 21st century. Trucking is used for 70 per cent of Ontario's exports to the U.S. and 75 per cent of our imports. Trucking is the lifeblood of our economy. It must be saved.
In closing, I cannot stress too strongly to this government that they are ignoring the people who are losing their jobs, their trucks, their homes, their families and their livelihood. My riding has been devastated.
Many thousands of truckers, including the hundreds here in Ottawa are just trying to make a living, but the government is tying their hands behind their backs. The recession is hitting hard. Give us a level playing field.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member for Kent for his comments on the nine suggestions proposed by the member for York West. The member for Kent obviously approves of them.
The indication was that the Leader of the Official Opposition also approved of them. As we have heard that this is not a problem that has occurred overnight, that it has been accumulating for over two or three years, I am wondering if the hon. member could tell me what

May 17, 1991
Supply
the cost of these particular suggestions that his party is making is.
Obviously the suggestions did not just come off the top of his head. I am sure his party has carefully analysed the particular cost of this program. Perhaps if the number is not at his fingertips some of his members could help him. Clearly this policy has been supported by the leader of his party. Could he give me some idea of the cost of these suggestions and whether the constituents in his riding of Kent support the use of taxpayers' money for these programs?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question. Certainly there will be a cost. The cost will be minimal relative to the returns created by people working. It is just the same as putting a man on welfare when he should be working. The return to the government would be much more with him working. The cost of what the truckers pay to run, for repairs, tires, and fuel and the people who are involved with them, whether truck-stop waitresses, mechanics, everyone that is supported by the truckers through their financial payments to them, all of this will come back to the government. The very little that we would be spending initially would be paid back many thousand times over.
I am happy to see we have the ex-minister of finance with us. If he could give me the figure on how much the GST is going to bring in, maybe I could elaborate further on how much money these suggestions would cost. I cannot give a figure right now. As the hon. member for York West mentioned, it is still in the study phase.
If the hon. trade minister could just give me the figures on the GST then maybe we could come up with a figure.

Mr. Speaker, we have taken a look at the cost. For instance, through the excise tax on diesel fuel, both in trucking and in aviation, this government raised approximately $300 million. That includes on aviation, so revenues from trucking are considerably less.
If we take a fraction of that $300 million, the revenue lost to the Treasury is very much a cost worth paying for an industry that directly employs 600,000 people across the country, a multi-billion dollar industry that is going down the drain. The cost of unemployment insurance,
the cost of welfare to those unemployed people, the cost of losing that infrastructure, the cost of losing 600,000 jobs, the cost of losing multiplier-effect jobs would be a heavier toll for this government to pay.
The government can either pay a cost now worth paying or face a much bigger cost later, after it has lost the industry. Perhaps the hon. member for Kent can make some comments based on this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate.
I want to pick up on a point that was a topic in Question Period earlier today. Two members were commenting on the cynicism with which Canadians are viewing their members of Parliament these days.
One of the reasons for that is there is too loose a use of so-called truth and a lot of use of myths. We can recall what the member for Etobicoke North said about the free trade agreement.
He said, back in 1988 or 1989: "Every sparrow that falls we are going to blame on the free trade agreement". This is just one of those examples. In the motion that was put today the Liberals have found another sparrow that they are going to blame on the free trade agreement.
I want to substantiate what I say, not with a few generalizations but with facts.
No one in this House is happy when they hear the stories of the truckers. My colleague, the Minister of Transport, has met with the truckers and their wives. They have spent a good amount of time talking about the difficulties that they are facing. We acknowledge and recognize those difficulties.
Let us find out, as members of Parliament, what is causing these difficulties. Let us go to the source of these difficulties and not base our statements on a number of myths.
May 17, 1991

My purpose today is to talk about the free trade agreement and its impact on the truckers. I cannot let the occasion go by without recalling for the House a decision that we took in the design of the goods and services tax on how we would treat the question of tax on gasoline.
We had a tax under the old tax system of 19 per cent. It was going to drop to 7 per cent under the new tax, but we felt that if we just dropped it to 7 per cent the provinces would take the revenue from the consumer. It would have probably been the easiest $500 million the provinces ever took.
We took a decision that we would keep the price to the consumer the same. We had two ways of doing that. One was to increase the excise tax. The other was to apply the GST on the provincial taxes, broaden the tax base and get more moneys out of the goods and services tax.
We took the second approach. The principal reason we took the second approach was that the tax paid under the goods and services tax could be recovered by people in the transportation industry so they would not have to pay that tax. If we had gained those revenues through the excise tax, we would not have been able to provide the truckers with the credit.
However, because we did it through the goods and services tax, they got the credit. I have heard, from the member for Hamilton East and from other members directly in front of me, that the GST is the the cause of the truckers' problems when the truckers are beneficiaries under the goods and services tax in two ways.
First, as I have just described, the truckers get a full credit on the GST paid in the cost of their fuel. They get it 21 days after they present their application or they get interest paid by the government.
The second reason that the truckers benefit from the GST is because under the old tax there was a hidden tax in the cost of a truck and in the cost of a trailer. All of that is recoverable under the GST so that their costs are being reduced.
They don't buy that.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
My friend from Chatham over here says that he does not buy that.
If he did not deal in myths, mistruths, or misinterpretation and distortion of the facts, then he would understand it. This is essentially the point that I want to make to my colleagues here in the House today so that we can
Supply
deal in the facts and not in distortions of the truth like we are hearing in the House today.
Madam Speaker, my role today is to talk about the free trade agreement. I have two principal points and then some examples to make.
My first point is that transportation, at the request of the Americans, was not a part of the free trade agreement. Therefore, there is nothing in the free trade agreement that applies to the trucking industry. I look at this motion today, which blames the problem on the free trade agreement. Now I hear the critic for transport for the Liberal Party saying that the problem started before that. He is saying it again, Mr. Speaker. The problem was before the free trade agreement came into effect. Then why did he make reference to the free trade agreement in the motion today? For what other reason?
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know it is raining outside, but there does not have to be a storm in here.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. That is my first point, that there is nothing in the free trade agreement that affects the trucking industry in a direct sense in either a positive or negative way.
The point I do want to make is that the volume of trade since 1988 has increased by about 12 per cent. That means business, because that trade has to move on various forms of transportation, including trucking.
Exports are up 12 per cent since 1988. Imports are up
11.6	per cent and the balance of trade is up from $14 billion surplus to a $17 billion surplus. So the basis for the business of the truckers has increased since the free trade agreement came in.
I hear again the member opposite saying that the free trade agreement had nothing to do with it. Then why is the reference in the motion that the free trade agreement is the cause of the problems of the truckers outside here? That is the sort of thing that breeds cynicism in the minds of Canadians today.
I also want to look a bit into the future and relate my comments to what some people are saying about the impact of the free trade agreement on their businesses, because we are hearing a broad range of stories from members opposite about lay-offs and plant closings that

May 17, 1991
Supply
they blame on the free trade agreement-more sparrows that fall that are blamed on the free trade agreement.
I want to talk about some people who are saying good things about the free trade agreement. I want to mention a company, Trimac of Calgary. Trimac is one of the largest trucking and service companies in Canada. They expected to see a greater amount of north-south traffic as a result of the free trade agreement, and Bud McCaig has said:
We anticipated that free trade would impact favourably on the bulk chemical transportation sector. Since we are the largest bulk carrier in Canada and well positioned on both sides of the border, we expected that it would impact positively on us as well. While it is difficult to quantify statistically right now, my feeling is that crossborder trade volumes are up, and that free trade has been positive.
Weyerhauser Canada's investments over the last two years at their plants in Prince Albert and Saskatoon have resulted in increased production destined for U.S. markets. The investments have also resulted in an increase in the firm's shipping volume. I want to quote here from Bill Gainer, vice-president of Weyerhauser. He says:
We are part of a competitive North American and world market. We have enhanced our competitiveness and we will be investing more.
Jay Lilje, president of Allied Van Lines, says his company's 1989 purchase, in a bid to capture opportunities offered by free trade of the Canadian operations of U.S. based Mayflower Transit Inc. have:
-strengthened Allied Van Line's transborder operations, which we see growing with free trade, and liberalization of cross-border movements.
He indicates that the company is quite pleased with the results of the acquisition, particularly in the context of the free trade agreement.
Construction is well advanced on Freightliner of Canada's new truck manufacturing facility in St. Thomas. Why would they be making trucks, Madam Speaker? Because people are buying trucks. According to company president John Mosier, the decision to build the St. Thomas factory, which will employ 1,100 people when completed, was taken as a direct result of the free trade agreement.
The point that I want to make here is that if we as members of Parliament are going to remove this element of cynicism which is poisoning the atmosphere in the economy and in society today, we have to deal with facts. I have demonstrated here how the free trade agreement has been a benefit for the Canadian economy, has been a benefit for the Canadian truckers.
There are problems. We acknowledge that, but let us get the facts right, let us get the facts on the table and make the decision based on the facts, not on the myths and distortions.
Hear, hear.

I have a very simple question to ask the hon. minister. Having cited the great benefits that have come to ordinary truckers in Canada, I wonder whether he would be willing, with me, to put on his raincoat and rain hat and walk out on to the steps in front of these buildings and talk to those people and tell them and their wives and their children how much free trade and deregulation has benefited them. Will you join me? I will meet you out there in five minutes.

Madam Speaker, this was an incredible feat. They go to their club house and they pull out the heavy hitters-just like they did in the 1988 campaign-and they were supposed to give us the truth and the facts. Here is a minister who strolls in and who rarely visits his riding and talks to average Canadians in Etobicoke Centre, and he has the audacity not only in the throne speech to say that the free trade deal has been the security blanket for the economy, but comes in here and suggests that somehow the free trade agreement has helped the truckers.
If the minister had cared to tune in this morning and early afternoon, he would have heard that the trucking industry was given away, was sacrificed before the free trade rounds. And what we had suggested, Mr. Minister, was that you would have had the duty and the responsibility if you had any concern during the free trade rounds to have equalized the two fields, to have obtained for our tuckers an adjustment program, just like your Prime Minister said during the 1988 campaign, just like you
May 17, 1991

said, sir, from the Atlantic to the Pacific .You said: "We will bring in the greatest adjustment programs in the western world".
I ask the minister, through the Chair, where are those programs that were promised in 1988? Where are those programs that the Prime Minister promised? Why does he not give us the truth and the facts rather than spinning out these false dreams that he has been spinning out for six years?
Another thing we said about the GST, again if the minister would have cared, is first, we urged the Minister of Transport to increase the time of those rebates. Does the minister know that since January 1 no trucking firm has received its GST rebates and, therefore, its cash flow hurts. The second thing we asked the Minister of Transport was to give the trucking companies extra time with which to remit their GST obtained from the shippers, because the trucking companies have to remit those receipts in 45 days, but the shipping companies don't pay the truckers until 50, 60 and 90 days. That is what we have said about the GST. Those are the facts. The minister is the myth maker and the dream breaker.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to talk about the adjustment programs. As a result of the change in the unemployment insurance program, we have introduced an increase of $550 million this year, which will grow to $750 million in two or three year's time, of increased amounts for training. These moneys will go to people who are out of jobs, who are looking for additional skills so they can get back into the labour force with better skills to get better jobs and better opportunities. That is on top of the $1.7 billion of the Canadian Jobs Strategy that we brought in in 1984.
I remind my hon. friend that back in 1984 almost the total amount of the moneys that were going into the job market were passive moneys, income support moneys, not active moneys, moneys that would help people gain better jobs through increased training.
The Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD, has done studies on this that show the change; show that we are still below where we should be relative to other countries. We have made a clear commitment, reinforced in the Speech from the Throne, to move in that direction. These are a funda-

mentally different set of policies than were followed by the Liberal Party before 1984.
My friend talked about the GST. I am advised that 70 per cent of the refund requests received thus far have been actioned within the 21 days. The other 30 per cent-
That could be false.
