speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the issue underlying today's motion, the competitive problems confronting our country's trucking industry, is one that deeply concerns me and every member of our government. The need for a dynamic, competitive transportation sector is real, not just for those who earn their living and support their families through this industry, but also because of the role it plays across the broad spectrum of Canada's economy.
But painful dilemmas will not be solved by political grandstanding, and you will not find effective answers by placing blame where it does not belong.
That is why I want to set the record straight for my hon. friends in the opposition concerning the federal tax system. It is not the source of the problem here today. In fact, because of the extensive tax reforms our government has put in place, this is one area where the trucking industry, and Canadian business in general, is better positioned today than it was just a few years ago.
I know there are people who do not want to believe that. Federal taxation makes a convenient target for those who would prefer to think there are easy, instant solutions for serious difficulties. But the facts tell a different story.
Truckers have identified higher diesel fuel costs in Canada as one of the critical disadvantages they face in competing with American firms both here and in the United States. It has been argued that federal taxes on

May 17, 1991
Supply
diesel fuel sales are a significant part of that burden, but that just is not true.
Instead, federal excise taxes on diesel fuel are actually lower in Canada than the federal tax in the United States, 4 cents a litre here compared to 6.2 cents there. In other words, Washington's taxes on diesel fuel are 50 per cent higher than ours.
The only other federal tax on fuel sales in Canada is the GST. And, yes, there is no equivalent federal tax south of the border. The GST is not a hobble on Canada's truckers, not a handicap they face. Instead of tilting the playing field in favour of American competitors, the GST has eliminated disadvantages created by previous Canadian governments through the destructive federal sales tax.
Under the GST, truckers recover every single cent of sales tax they pay on fuel used for business purposes. That means that the GST does not add to fuel costs.
This is not the only benefit the GST delivers, as the minister just said. Under the old manufacturers' sales tax, Canadian businesses, including truckers, ended up paying tax that was included in the price of many goods and services they needed to run their operations.
Some of those costs were direct, such as the telecommunications service tax. Others were less visible, but they were still there. This was because the producers of goods and services paid the FST on many of the items they used to do business and passed them on their customers. But that does not happen under the GST.
Through the use of the input tax credit, businesses at every level now recover all the tax they pay on their commercial transactions. There is no hidden tax passed on through this system. This has already reduced the cost of many items and is helping service providers, such as maintenance garages and mechanics, control their costs and prices. This is helping Canadians compete, not put them at a disadvantage.
There is another issue that truckers have raised and I want to review it. They have pointed out correctly that Canadian tax depreciation rates on tractors and trailers are not as generous as those in the United States.
However, that criticism overlooks that the U.S. truckers must pay a 12 per cent excise tax on the purchase of
heavy trucks and trailers. There is no such tax in Canada. This more than offsets the faster depreciation available in the United States.
The facts I have just outlined are the bottom line realities. They provide dollar and cents evidence that federal excise taxes, the GST and depreciation schedules have not sacrificed the interests of domestic transporters. As Monday's Speech from the Throne made clear, this is a government committed to helping Canadians meet competitive challenges, so we can all benefit from that success.
But this does not mean that truckers are crying wolf about the total tax burden on fuel purchases. American prices are lower and state level taxation is a definite contributing factor. We have to confront the fact that provincial taxes on diesel fuel can run double or more than those in neighbouring American states.
Earlier this year if you fuelled up your truck in British Columbia, you paid 11.4 cents a litre in provincial tax. In Washington State, across the border, it was 6.8 cents.
In Saskatchewan you paid 10 cents, 5.3 cents in North Dakota.
In Ontario you were paying 10.9 cents compared to just
4.6	cents a litre in Michigan.
In Quebec, it was 13.5 cents a litre, four times higher than the 3.1 cents that the same trucker would be paying in New York State.
Following the recent provincial budget, this disparity has become even worse. Ontario's tax on diesel was boosted 1.7 cents with an equal increase due next January.
In reviewing these figures, I am not trying to suggest that provincial governments alone have the responsibility for assisting our freight trucking section to deal with their problems. This is a national problem and one that will only be resolved through mutual commitment and partnership by all levels of government working with the industry, much as the task forces the previous minister set up and the current minister is dealing with.
Let me also suggest a basic, critical principle that we must apply to identifying answers. That is, the solution must not be based on actions that would jeopardize our ability to stay the course in holding down our deficit
May 17, 1991

during difficult times and bringing it down dramatically once economic growth is fully restored.
I know my hon. friends across the floor do not share that view. Spending restraint is not a prescription that they are familiar with. We saw that during the 1981-1982 recession, when our deficit doubled in just two years and then continued to grow as we entered recovery, reaching $38.5 billion a year in 1984-85. The all time record.
Today we are still living with the consequences of those deficits and the $200 billion national debt we inherited. If it was not for the for the interest payments on that debt, we would not be in the deficit position now and we would have the resources to better help the many individuals and business sectors that have been hit hard by another recession.
Just last year, $43 billion in Canadian taxpayers' dollars went just to pay the interest charges on the debt. That is $43 billion that could have been used to lower the debt or lower taxes, $43 billion that was not available to increase unemployment insurance entitlements or for education and apprenticeship programs or to contribute to funding health care programs or to boost family allowances and pensions. That is the part of the tragedy of deficits and debt left to us by the Liberal government.
There is another aspect to that tragedy, one that ties directly to the competitive challenges faced by truckers and virtually every other business sector. The blunt fact is deficits and debt contribute to inflation and to inflationary expectations and by doing so put further pressure on interest rates. There is no member in this House who has not heard our constituents, individuals, local businesses and industry associations say that lower interest rates are essential to get the economy moving and reduce investment costs. But, as the February budget so clearly described, the only way rates can be brought down and kept down is to reduce inflation. To do that, government must play its part, including keeping its own costs under control. [DOT]
Our policies are working. Inflation has stabilized and interest rates have dropped 5 per cent in the last year. Controlling spending does not come easily. There are always ways in which to spend more, always groups and interests, such as the troubled trucking sector, with real problems who can make passionate and convincing
Supply
appeals for assistance. However, good economic management and real leadership mean a striking and realistic balance between specific sectors and interests and the needs of the wider, national community, including taxpayers.
It is clear that Canadians feel they are already taxed too much. They do not want governments to go deeper into debt with the automatic consequences that tax burdens will rise in the future.
This takes me back to the issue of taxation and its impact on truckers and other industries challenged to compete in the North American and international markets.
There are a couple of issues here I would like to touch on briefly in my final moments. Since first coming to office in 1984, our government has recognized the need to ensure our total national tax system did not place Canadians at a competitive disadvantage. At the same time, we were also committed to improving the fairness of the tax system and maintaining its ability to support the programs and services Canadians value.
We acted on this commitment, not just through the GST, but also through extensive reforms to the personal and corporate income tax systems that took effect in
1988.	We are convinced that those reforms have delivered real benefits.
Again, I realize this seems to be a fly in the face of conventional public wisdom. There seems to be a common misunderstanding that we are among the most heavily taxed nations in the world. In particular, Canadians often point to the United States and see it as a taxation nirvana. Figures from the Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development, the OECD, in 1988, the last year that figures were available, paint a somewhat different picture. On an international basis, the figures show that the burden of total taxation in Canada, by all levels of government, amounted to 34 per cent of our gross domestic product. This was actually lower than 16 of the 24 OECD countries. In fact, among the major group of seven industrial nations, only Japan and the United States had taxes as low as ours. In Japan, taxation was equal to 31.3 per cent of GDP, while in the U.S. it was 29.8 per cent. That was not dramatically lower than our 34 per cent.

May 17, 1991
Supply
While there are many aspects to the relationship between taxes and business, it is a fact that Canadian companies do not face as great a competitive handicap as many would like to believe.
But with respect to our competitiveness with the United States, we have to face the reality that American productivity has grown much stronger than ours in recent years and Canadian labour costs now exceed theirs. Factors like this go a long way to explaining why Canadian firms and workers are finding it harder to compete.
However, there is another aspect to the tax story that we also need to remind ourselves of on a regular basis. We have agreed, as a nation, to allocate tax resources so that every Canadian has access to public health care. We also provide further resources to cover the cost of post-secondary education. Both of these are areas where America places the bulk of the burden on the individual and the private sector.
I do not know of many, if any, Canadians who would trade our medicare system for that in the U.S. The cost of private health care insurance is something that is frequently overlooked when critics compare our tax levels to those of American firms.
I do not want to shift today's debate away from the real problems Canadian truckers face. They are serious, there is a hardship, and we need to look at the problem seriously. However, I know it is essential that, in developing a strategy, this House and all interested Canadians recognize that there is no simple, quick fix solutions that our government can impose by fiat. The perception that the federal taxation is the source of the problem is based on wishful thinking or partisan politics- not fact. Any prescriptions based on such a misunderstanding will run the real risk of missing the mark and could even damage our prospects to strengthen our competitiveness as a nation.

Madam Speaker, the idle trucks that are lined up just outside the door here along Wellington Street are really just a microcosm of Canada's labour force. They represent Canada's unemployed men and women. It just happens to be the truckers. That just happens to be the transportation industry in Canada. That is the industry which moves the nation. When that stops, as it has stopped today, it says so much about the inner workings of a nation. It says a once proud occupation has been silenced, that of the truckers, the guys who took pride in their rigs pounding down the nation's highways. They have been silenced
because of the mismanagement of the current government and its economic policies.
This is not because they wanted to be silenced. Their rigs are in good shape and they are ready to go, so that is not the problem. They have kept their rigs in good shape because it is a proud occupation and they know that they are in a very competitive business. They know that the tax write-off on their equipment is spread over many years, unlike their U.S. competitors who can write theirs off in a matter of four years or so. They know that they are working at a terrible disadvantage because their competitors can get an annual tax break of several thousands of dollars on the purchase of that very expensive equipment.
They know too that they are trying to survive in an industry when their competitors in the U.S. can buy diesel fuel for slightly more than half the price they pay in Canada. In spite of these handicaps, they would like to keep on trucking, as they say.
However, now they cannot because every mile they drive means they are losing money and time has run out. When they buy a tank of diesel fuel they do not stop to think how much is tax and how much is cost. They only know one figure and that is the one that is registered up on the pump. That is what they pay.
All they hear from the new Minister of Transport is: "You'll have to become more competitive". It is pretty hard to be competitive if you do not have any money in your pocket. This is a government that has its hands in all four of their pockets, right up to the elbow in most cases, and then the minister says: "Come on boys, be more competitive".
Instead of losing more money than they have already lost they decided to park their rigs out on Wellington Street. I talked to one young man outside the other day. He said he would like to be back at work. I asked him how he could afford to have his rig parked here. He said: "If it wasn't parked here, it would be parked somewhere else". It does not really matter to him whether it is parked on Wellington Street or parked outside his home.
These people are really representative of Canada's labour force today. They are disappointed. They are disillusioned that their lives and that of their families have been turned around so suddenly. "Gone are the days", they say, "when there was work out there to be done" and they were willing to do it. They met the payments on their equipment. They took great pride in what they did well and the knowledge that they would be
May 17, 1991

able to look after the needs of their families in those good years.
It just happens to be truckers that have ascended outside the door here recently. It could have been the farmers of this nation. They have been burdened and bludgeoned by debt for so long that they have become discouraged and disillusioned the same as the truckers.
A callous government is how they described the Tory government, as one which does not seem to understand just how tenuous their livelihood is, whether it is trucking or farming these days in Canada.
Instead of truckers or farmers, it could have been the small town merchants, the restaurant owners and the gas station operators of this nation, who just like the truckers are watching their lifestyles disappear as economic conditions in Canada due to the GST, the high dollar, the high interest rate and the over-all cost of doing business in this country has forced their regular customers, their neighbours to go to a foreign country on a regular basis to do their shopping.
All this is happening in spite of the government having studies over a year ago indicating that these devastations of our economy were on the horizon if the government failed to alter their economic policies.
The government knew this was going to happen and sat idly by. It is unfortunate that the truckers have to illustrate their plight in the manner we see out in front of the Parliament Buildings, but I want to congratulate them for their ingenuity. If that is what it takes to get the government's attention, perhaps the truckers' efforts are not in vain after all. We will have to wait and see.
The government's tax policies and fiscal measures have resulted in 1.4 million Canadians being unemployed. After a Speech from the Throne just a few days ago with no new measures in it, none whatsoever, to suggest that the government is even cognizant of the malaise that has fallen over Canada, what alternatives do the truckers have?
I think the truckers with their rigs standing still are symbolic. They are a reflection of so many aspects of
Supply
Canadian life today. Perhaps it is time for the government to admit what the overwhelming majority of Canadians already know, that this government has caused the nation to come to a halt and is now completely barren of any new initiatives which could get the wheels of the nation turning once again.
Perhaps it is time for the government to be honest with Canadians just this one time. Perhaps the government could admit it has no programs to offer, resign and call an election so Canadians can once more be given a choice.
I think-and the polls would support me-that given a choice today, Canadians would choose to bury the remnants of this government and opt for a government with a new set of priorities for all Canadians.
They would opt for a new government whose number one priority is to address the very real problems of doing business in this country today. The very real problems are dramatically symbolized by the idle rigs outside the House of Commons at this very moment. It is so un-Canadian to have these men and women sitting idle when they would like to get their equipment to work.
They would like to put their expertise and their energies to work but they cannot do it. It is a losing cause.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of my colleague who just spoke.
The representation that he is making today on behalf of the truckers is not new. The Liberal Party, the opposition, has opposed deregulation. We said, years ago, that deregulation would be bad for the trucking industry.
Certainly on numerous occasions, we intervened before the House to indicate the danger of deregulation in Canada. Indeed, it has put our trucking industry in a very difficult position vis-a-vis the American trucking industry.
Would my colleague comment on some of the proposals that have been put forward by our party in this debate in order to help the government a solution to this problem?

May 17, 1991
Supply
On behalf of the Official Opposition, the member for York West put forward a proposal today that is extremely important and could help the government find a solution to the problems of the trucking industry.
I would like to ask my colleague to elaborate on this proposal put forward by our colleague from York West.

Madam Speaker, I have a copy of that paper which my colleague presented earlier today.
When it comes to something like deregulation, we are still a northern nation. We live along a little ribbon around the 49th parallel, but the bulk of Canada is in more extreme weather conditions than exists anywhere in the United States.
We have to realize what is practical, in terms of competing, lake, for example, the dairy industry. Anyone who thinks that we can compete with the dairy industry in southern Virginia probably does not know anything about the dairy industry. Go down there and watch that industry in mass production.
They can make it from some of those places in the United States into Canada. It is a long overnight haul. One of those trucks could bring a litre of milk for every man, woman, and child in my riding in one trip. Can we compete with that? Anyone who thinks we can does not know the dairy industry and what is necessary to compete.
That is typical I think. Canadians say: "We can compete. We are honest, hard working people". Of course, we are honest, hard working people but we have to be realistic. There are areas in which we can compete and there are areas in which we cannot compete.
I do not think we can compete in the transportation industry, not when we see these fellows waiting out there. They cannot compete. They cannot let a fellow who can fill up his tank and save a couple of hundred dollars come across, take away their livelihood, and compete with that.
I wish the government would put it in terms that I could understand. I would try to understand, if the government could explain it to me. I cannot understand. I do not understand how anyone could think we could compete in the dairy industry either. I know enough about it. I know that we cannot compete. The government should realize that there are areas in which we can compete and that is not one of them. I do not think we can compete in this area, with the deregulation as it applies to the transportation industry, either.
The Tories talk about the GST as a great success story, the free trade agreement as a great success story. Canadians had better not accept too many more of these Tory success stories. They have resulted in 1.4 million people being unemployed. It is just too much. We cannot take any more Tory success stories.

Madam Speaker, I speak today in this debate with much regret and bitterness, because this debate reminds me of debates we had here in this House in 1987 when the Conservative government insisted on presenting Bills C-18 and C-19 which at that time seemed to us in the Opposition to be a death sentence for the whole trucking industry in Canada.
Despite our objections, despite the repeated requests from this side of the House to delay that bill, unless we had guarantees from the Americans, the then-Minister of Transport went ahead with his bill, with the consequences we see today.
We are not glad to see these truckers occupy part of Wellington Street here in Ottawa and protest as they are doing on the highways of Ontario. These truckers are suffering unfair competition from American truckers. We in the opposition had warned the government three years ago that this would happen, and we were not the only ones to say so.
I refer you to a debate that took place on February 5, 1987, where, in a statement I made then, I repeated the words of Gerry Reimer, Vice-President of Reimer Express Lines of Winnipeg, and I quote what he said then: "American companies can come here and cut rates to smithereens for a year or two and all domestic truckers will be gone."
I would also like to quote a leading Canadian business executive, Mr. John Kennedy, the president of Kingsway Transport, of Rexdale, Ontario, who said in 1987: "There is no doubt that deregulation will have disastrous effects on the financial position of the trucking industry in
May 17, 1991

Canada. Ultimately, it will lead to a wave of mergers, takeovers and bankruptcies."
Madam Speaker, three or four years later, we find ourselves in a situation where Canadian truckers are giving up hope of getting any assistance from the Conservative government. At the time, the government refused to listen to the industry, and to the opposition members who opposed these bills and were telling it that deregulation would be harmful to the trucking industry. They were saying that tens of thousands of jobs would be lost if the government were to implement deregulation.
So today, about three and a half years later, we find ourselves with the terrible conclusion that, indeed, approximately 35,000 to 40,000 jobs have been lost in the trucking industry in Canada, jobs that we will never get back, that are now in the United States, that have been lost in Canada because of the incompetence of the Conservative government. Those were jobs that allowed thousands of Canadian families to make a decent living here in Canada and that were totally lost to American transportation companies competing with Canadian companies, with the approval and the blessing of the Conservative government.
Madam Speaker, it is obvious that today something must be done before the whole industry disappears, as suggested by representatives of the trucking industry three and a half years ago. It seems obvious to me that if the government has no other alternatives than to study this issue over and over again, it should immediately implement the proposals made by my colleague from York West, who has specific proposals to assist representatives of the trucking industry who are here in Ottawa. What they want from the government is not studies, but decisions that will solve their problems and save the thousands of jobs which still exist in the Canadian trucking industry.
Obviously, one of the worst problems was that according to Bill C-19, the government at the time proposed that businesses drop the public convenience and necessity criterion. I must recall that the criterion existed in Canada since 1954 for the very purpose of protecting the trucking industry. The criterion was effective, as, between 1960 and 1970, the Canadian trucking industry
Supply
prospered and rendered great services, not only to our country, but to thousands of its workers.
But, at the request of some important shippers, a few companies, obviously very rich, very important and very close to the government, deregulation was brought in, without regards to the small truckers' interests, but to please a few big shippers in Canada. That is what happened, again. It is easy to understand: a Conservative govemement listens to the big and the wealthy in our society, but it remains completely deaf to the interests of the less fortunate. So, it agreed to the request of the big shippers and proceeded with deregulating a Canadian industry which was then in good shape. But that is not the case anymore, because deregulation here produced exactly the same results as in the United States where it had been implemented a few years before, supposedly to allow for more competition on the marketplace.
But, what did we see in the United States? Over there, deregulation favoured the largest companies. Four very large companies are controlling almost all the trucking market in United States and today, they literarily gobble up the small trucking companies in Canada.
We said all that in 1987 to a Conservative government who did not want to listen. Today, we live with the consequences of this harmful, completely inappropriate and unacceptable policy of the Conservative government. Today, we tell them: For God's sake, stop your useless studies and do something. Follow the recommendations of our colleague from York West, solve the problems of the truckers and save the few jobs left in this industry.

I, myself, spent an extra two hours on highway 2 trying to get through in order to avoid highway 104.1 also spent a very short period after I got on to highway 104 at Port Union Road all the way over to Yonge Street viewing the suffering of people trying to get home.
It was an extremely impressive demonstration. There were enormous trucks as far as the eye could see and

there were enormous numbers of frustrated motorists. Every single arterial road in my riding was clogged.
There was the possibility of very serious consequences. North York General Hospital, which is at the edge of my riding, has the highest volume emergency department in Canada and that hospital had one of the major access roads to it clogged.
I think that this was an incredible demonstration that should never be repeated. I think the truckers are certainly right in their frustration at the lack of co-operation of government in Canada.
Consumers do not want to pay more for goods and services in Canada than they would in the United States. Clearly, they are voting with their feet. If we do not get our industries competitive, we are going to lose a lot of business and people will move to the United States and industry will leave.
This issue is one that is important to us all and very important to consumers. If there are those who think that regulating the industry and protecting the transportation industry in order to keep out competition is the way to go, they are very, very wrong. It is impossible in the global marketplace. It is key to many of the industries in Canada.
Transportation costs are high throughout Canada, and we have got to get those costs lower. We have been trying, at the federal level with our government, to lower those costs. Clearly, the GST, as the minister has explained, has been extremely helpful. One thing that has to be done to help truckers and other businesses is for the provincial governments to harmonize with the GST. Right away, they could give an enormous rebate to many of these truckers so they could compete because American truckers would also have to pay the GST on any services delivered in Canada and it is fully rebatable.
Look at the tax situation. The taxes at the federal level are much, much lower than the Americans and the problem is at the provincial level. The provincial governments are gouging. When you look at Ontario, we have had a budget that has shown no restraint; 5.8 per cent increase in civil servants' wages. That goes all the way through the economy.
I know people at Metropolitan Toronto Council are talking about the fact that they cannot do anything less with the civil servants there. It is an extremely difficult
circumstance and what we have to do is become more competitive.

Madam Speaker, a short answer to the intervention of the hon. member would be what Kevin Ford, a married father of three, who drives for a small Guelph, Ontario hauler, said here yesterday when he was interviewed by the press. He said: "There are days when you have to work 20 hours to make ends meet". This trucker had to give up his house and two cars to keep his family afloat.
There are some inconveniences to people who live in residential Toronto, but you have to think of these drivers who also had homes but because of the incompetence of the Conservative government have lost their homes. If the government had moved earlier on this matter there would be no blockage today.
Last year in the summer, independent truckers blocked several border crossings in Ontario and Quebec to draw attention to the problem they have with U.S. truckers paying less for their rigs, fuels, parts, maintenance and insurance.
The then Minister of Transport decided to study the matter. He established a study that was to cover seven points. This week, the new Minister of Transport is telling us that the study is not finished, that it might not be finished before sometime next year. Well surely these truckers want action and they are not going to-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on trucking as there is a need to set the record straight, particularly about as what was just said a few minutes ago across the floor.
There is a need, as well, to explain the enormous amount of complex work that has gone on over the past 12 months.
During the past few days, hon. members of the opposition have criticized the government for its approach taken over the past year. This is not unusual or unexpected. The government has been following an approach of careful targeting of the issue; a difficult job with a moving target. It has been doing this with the
May 17, 1991

agreement and support of a large segment of the trucking industry.
During the past week, we have witnessed a number of demonstrations by truckers here in Ottawa and elsewhere which had their genesis in a series of demonstrations which began in Quebec in mid-May 1990. Then, a group of independent truckers demonstrated by blocking highways and the border crossing at Lacolle.
The Quebec Minister of Transport listened to the demands of these independent truckers and agreed to set up a commission to study their demands. The creation of the commission had been one of the principal requests of the truckers themselves.
The provincial minister invited the participation of the federal government in the work of the commission, and in recognizing the shared jurisdiction between the federal government and the provincial government in extra provincial trucking matters, the former Minister of Transport agreed. A senior official of the department participated fully in all the deliberations of what came to be known as the Charbonneau commission.
Approximately one week after the Quebec truckers demonstrated, a group calling itself "Canadian Truckers Fighting Back" blocked the Ambassador Bridge in Windsor. Another sympathetic group closed additional international crossing in southern Ontario at Sarnia, Fort Erie, Niagara Falls and Gananoque.
The Ontario Minister of Transportation agreed to meet the blockaders at Windsor, because of the extreme importance of that transportation link to the health of the Canadian automobile industry.
The auto industry in southern Ontario and in the U.S., which relies on just-in-time delivery, was rapidly coming to a stand still because of the bridge closures. Once again, recognizing the shared federal-provincial responsibility in international trucking issues, the federal government responded quickly and effectively. The former Minister of Transport flew overnight to Windsor and met with the truckers in the early morning to get to the bottom of their complaints.
After several hours of discussions, the demonstrators agreed that the cancellation of the free trade agreement and the setting aside of the deregulation of the trucking
Supply
industry were not responsible or reasonable proposals, which shows that the truckers themselves were a little more reasonable than some of the members opposite.
A short list of action items was adopted which the minister agreed to raise with his federal colleagues and best efforts were assured.
These issues were:
(1)	U.S. carriers doing cabotage in Canada.
(2)	Unfair, even predatory pricing practices by U.S. carriers.
(3)	Collection of federal fuel taxes from U.S. carriers.
Also during the meeting in Windsor, the Minister of Transport agreed with the Ontario Minister of Transportation that a federal official be nominated to the Ontario Ministry of Transportation's Trucking Industry Adjustment Committee.
This provincial committee had been struck several weeks earlier to address the rising industry concerns which eventually culminated in the blockade.
The Ministers of Employment and Immigration and National Revenue were asked to investigate and report on cabotage.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was asked to investigate the alleged unfair pricing practices and the Minister of National Revenue was also asked to investigate the possibility of collecting federal excise taxes from U.S. carriers.
The Minister of Transport met representatives of owner operators and the three major trucking unions in Ottawa on June 27, 1990. At that time progress was reported on the three issues.
Stepped up enforcement of existing laws and regulations against illegal cabotage would be undertaken in conjunction with the provinces. Several blitzes have been conducted during the past year in co-operation with provincial authorities.
The issue of collecting federal tax on diesel fuel and its application to all trucking operations in Canada have been examined by the Department of Finance. It concluded that federal taxes on fuel are not a significant factor in the fuel price differences, vis-a-vis the United States. I think that has been amply illustrated today during the speeches.

May 17, 1991
Supply
At the time, diesel fuel sold in Canada was subject to Departmental officials were instructed to work with total federal sales tax and excise taxes of 6.8 cents per any newly formed owner-operator organization, to en-litre, about 2.8 cents and 4 cents per litre, respectively, sure they would meet this minimum criteria.
The former federal sales tax has since been replaced by the goods and services tax, as of January 1,1991. Since then, Canadian truckers have been able to fully recover the GST paid on diesel fuel. The result has been a net reduction in the total federal tax on diesel fuel, from 6.8 cents to 4 cents per litre.
Under the GST, the federal sales tax paid by truckers on fuel in Canada is significantly less than the comparable U.S. tax.
On the predatory pricing issue, the transport minister said that he was advised by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that the director of investigations and research under the Competition Act would examine any information brought to his attention regarding possible violations of the act.
During a meeting in May with the truckers, they had been advised to report their complaints to the director. Since then, the director has indicated that he has not yet received any new complaints or information that would raise an issue under the Competition Act.
At the conclusion of the June 27 meeting with the three major trucking unions and the representatives of the owner-operators, the minister decided to set up a ministerial level task force to examine the issues in depth.
Membership on the task force was open to all bona fide identifiable stakeholders in trucking: unions, carriers, shippers, and owner-operator organizations. The provinces and any involved federal government departments were invited to participate as observers so that the task force would be composed of all the stakeholders, with government only there in an observing position.
With respect to the owner-operator organization, modest organizational requirements were imposed upon them, basically to ensure that they had identifiable membership and an elected executive, that is, people they had agreed would speak on their behalf.
August 13 and August 14 were decided upon as the meeting dates in Toronto. The task force met as scheduled in August and was chaired in its entirety by the minister. In attendance were representatives from 16 industry groups. Five issues were distilled out of the two days of very frank, open discussions which the minister promised to take to his provincial colleagues at a meeting at the end of September.
Those issues were cabotage, Canada-U.S. tax regimes, driver education and training, uniformity of safety and other regulations, and load broker regulation. Although a strong consensus was reached at the task force meeting, there was a sense among the members that they did not share a common information base or even a common understanding of why an issue was important to a particular group within the stakeholder group.
Timely facts on trucking in Canada, especially facts on international trucking, are hard to come by. This realization was one of the reasons the task force agreed to conduct a comprehensive set of studies after the Council of Ministers meeting.
At the September meeting of the federal-provincial Ministers of Transport, the provincial ministers, without exception, committed themselves to work with the federal government in order to enhance cabotage enforcement. The provincial ministers also reviewed their commitment to uniform trucking regulations and pledged provincial support for the employment and immigration committee on driver training.
Last, but not least, they agreed to set up a working group to study owner-operator issues-items such as load broker regulation, the need for an industry standard code of ethics to govern carrier to owner-operator relationships, and so on.
The working group of officials set to work immediately and over the past seven or eight months has worked hard and consulted widely. They are due to present a report at the end of this month.
If there is a negative note to these efforts, it is that the carrier associations have consistently and steadfastly refused to co-operate on the issue of their relationship with the owner-operators.
May 17, 1991

The reason they advance for not participating in the discussions is that they have no mandate to undertake labour negotiations since they are in the domain of the direct discussions of individual trucking companies.
This is, in my view, a narrow and somewhat legalistic interpretation of the problem. While we have succeeded in convincing the two senior levels of government and the National Coalition of Owner-Operator Associations to sit down and hammer out a model code of practice, the Canadian Trucking Association has stayed away. Nevertheless, it is not too late to join in the process and I sincerely hope they will reconsider their position.
Let me turn now to the studies, as much has been made in this House over the last few days, and especially this afternoon, about the set of studies being undertaken by the minister's task force. As I mentioned earlier, one of the major frustrations surrounding the discussion of the Canadian trucking industry is the virtually complete lack of reliable information, statistical or otherwise. Consequently, the task force agreed to embark upon a set of studies which would rectify this problem.
The objectives of the study are very straightforward and are threefold: first, to determine the nature and extent of the Canadian trucking share of the trans-border markets; to assess the over-all competitiveness of Canadian trucking firms in those trans-border markets; and, to analyse the relative significance of factors affecting that competitiveness.
The project comprises the following individual study components: a survey of trans-border movements at approximately 15 major crossing points across Canada, a review of trends in trans-border trucking markets and a thorough examination of Canadian shares in those markets, an analysis of the economics of the Canadian trucking industry operating in trans-border markets, an examination of the current financial status of Canadian trucking firms, a comparison of Canadian and U.S. trucking costs in trans-border markets, a review of Canada-U.S. tax regimes, and an assessment of a potential Canada-U.S. cabotage agreement. There is also to be a final study to draw together the threads of the individual detailed studies.
At this point I wish to emphasize the complete openness that has been adopted in the conduct of these
Supply
studies. While federal officials have normally chaired the meetings, the task force members have selected the consultants, commented on the draft reports and are currently in the process of reviewing the final text of most of the studies. A session is being scheduled for early June to put the finishing touches on these studies, not next year as was mentioned earlier by the opposition.
Frankly, while we are duty bound to honour the process that we have started with the task force, that is to allow them the last word on the study contents, we will be very pleased to make these reports public so as to lay to rest the simple minded remarks of the members opposite.

speechtext:

We are concerned about the future of Canada. We are concerned about the children of the present and the future. The problems we are facing in this country today and the reasons for some of these lay-offs that have had to take place are due to the fact that we have some very difficult fiscal problems in this country.

May 17, 1991

Some of these fiscal problems were started years ago when other governments attempted to fight recessions by spending, spending, spending. They were not spending those days' dollars. They were spending today's dollars, tomorrow's dollars, our children's and our grandchildren's dollars.
The Government of Ontario, run by a party which is the same as the party this member belongs to, is doing the very same thing in Ontario today that did not work for Canada in 1981-82, will not work for Ontario today and it is adding to the problems of this country.
I have children and I want to see them have a future. I want the Canadians of today to have jobs. That is why we are making the difficult economic decisions that have to be made to make us competitive in a global marketplace. We cannot build a wall around Canada and live by supplying the Canadian market only.
We can survive only by being competitive in a global market. Being competitive means working smarter and addressing problems, not by throwing money at them. That is the easy way out.
Any government can throw money it does not have by continuing to borrow on the future to try to solve a problem. Throwing money at problems does not solve them. Working at problems is what solves the problems of this country. Working together, management, labour, government and education. We cannot be competitive in this country if we do not have well-trained young people.
We cannot have our young people dropping out of school because they do not have a challenge, because they are not taught properly and because they are not given proper advice by the counsellors in the schools. We cannot be driving all our children into university educations.
We have to look at the trades. I attended a Skills Canada training competition last weekend in my riding, which brought together 200 students from across this country. They were building framings for housing. They were repairing motors. They were working on tin plates to fix furnaces and piping. They were working on electronic boards.
They were competing in a skills competition which proves that we have well skilled young people in this country who want to get involved in the jobs of the future
that are high-skilled. They are going to Louisville, Kentucky to compete. Canadians went last year and there was only one state in the U.S. that got more medals than Canada did at that competition.
They did it because we have young people who are interested in the skills and trades and who want to have jobs in the future. You cannot have jobs in the future of this country if you throw away the money today.
That is why we are taking very hard economic decisions. They are not easy. We do not like to sit here, make decisions and then read in the paper the next day that
1,000	jobs have been lost.
You do not have a monopoly on compassion in the NDP or in the socialist party of this country. There is as much compassion on this side of the House as there is on that side of the House.
We sat here and read statements about the Minister for International Trade from people who were saying: "Yes, there are problems with free trade in some industries but it is also helping industries."
The opposition members say: "That's bull." It is bull when they do not believe in it. When they get up and make false statements, they think they are speaking the truth. One does not hear those comments from this side of the House, at least not from the members who are here today.
We have no monopoly on behaviour in this House. If there were a little more decorum in this House, Canadians might start to believe a little more that we do things in this House.
That decorum comes from all sides of the House. It is something that all members should pay very special attention to. All members from all parties have a responsibility in this House to show the young people in this country that decisions that are made in this House are very important. That is why, as the Prime Minister said, this is the constituent assembly of Canada, this is where the decisions are going to be made, and this is where they are made with a great deal of heart, consideration and understanding, regardless of what the opposition says.
We are talking about governments in general. When the people of Canada don't believe in governments it is not only the government in power that they don't believe

in, it is all politicians, because of the behaviour of all politicians. We all have a role to play.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
When it comes to the cabotage issue, as I mentioned in my remarks, there was co-operation between the provinces and the federal government in looking at cabotage.
I would just like to read, if I may, the following:
There were 2,862 truckers who passed inspection stations. Of these, 344 truckers, both American and Canadian, were referred to the custom officials. Of eight of the ten customs infractions discovered, only two involved cabotage, but all ten involved Canadian companies using U.S. vehicles illegally. Five hundred American drivers were checked for immigration infractions, 11 were found to have minor criminality infractions and two others were arrested and removed under escort for serious criminality infractions. No infractions involving cabotage by U.S. drivers were found.
In Manitoba, during the summer of 1990, an RCMP officer while on regular duty laid a charge against a U.S. driver for cabotage. Some half dozen letters had been received from owner-operators in trucking companies reporting incidents of suspected cabotage. These have all been referred to customs or immigration for action. We have been sending information out outlining Canadian immigration laws to U.S. drivers at border entry points. The same pamphlets are being mailed by Transport Canada to U.S. carriers licensed to operate in Canada to
Supply
make sure that they understand the laws of Canada when it comes to cabotage and our custom regulations.
As to the 3,300 additional licences that my hon. friend mentioned, I am afraid I do not have the facts to confirm that. Certainly, if there have been 3,300 additional licences in Ontario alone that have been issued at this time of what appears to be an over-supply on the market, I would wonder at the provincial government issuing those licences.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today and before I get into the comments about the motion brought forward by the Official Opposition I want to publicly congratulate the new Minister of Transport and the recycled Minister of State for Transport in their new positions. I look forward to working with them.
I want to suggest that today's debate, what has been happening outside this building on the streets of Ottawa, what has been happening on the streets and highways of Toronto and what has been happening at the Ambassador Bridge, is not just about transport. It is not just about trucking.
It is an indication of the kind of anger that has been building in this country since 1984. It is an anger over the way in which the Conservative Party as the Government
of Canada has been changing this country. It is intertwined between taxation, deregulation, the free trade agreement with the United States, the impending Cana-da-U.S.-Mexico free trade agreement, the cuts to VTA Rail, the cuts to CBC, the cuts to Canada Post and privatization, and it is almost as if people began to wake up in the last two or three months and said "My God what has happened to us? What have they done to us?"
The truckers, unlike most of us, have found the tool by which to express that anger. They have the vehicles which can be used to occupy space on roads, to blockade highways and entranceways, they have the tool by which to express their anger. In some ways, it is no different than what the workers at the Caterpillar plant did when they saw their jobs being lost and their factory being closed and sent to the United States: they occupied that space.
I want to suggest, very strongly, that if concrete steps are not taken soon to deal with the very legitimate grievances of the truckers, whether it be the owner-operators or the trucking companies and their employees, more and more Canadians will find their own way to express their visible anger to the Government of Canada.
It is important that the government works diligently to do that because I do not want to see this escalate. It is not in the best interest of the economy of this country. Politically it may be the best thing that could have happened in many, many years because it would put the pressure on the government to reverse the direction it has been taking us into, but other people will lose if it does accelerate.
I have met with the truckers and I have met with their spouses and their children and they have had it up to here. They have been waiting for the federal government for a year to take some concrete action. Instead, the government has got studies, it has promises of action and then decisions which say: "Well, it is really a minor item so we are not going to worry about it." It may be a minor item, but it is one more straw on the backs of these men and women whom we need to carry our raw materials and our finished products to market, whether within Canada or in the U.S. We have not been treating them fairly.

When this government deregulated trucking a number of years ago, it did not just match what the United States did, it went even farther by giving American truckers access to Canada without getting reciprocal agreements with the United States, putting our people at a disadvantage.
The anger is real, the frustration is real and the hardship is real.
The Minister of State for Transport, in her answer to my colleague, talked about tomorrow's children and tomorrow's grandchildren and that is why the government has embarked on this deficit reduction approach to managing this country. She pooh-poohed what Floyd Laughren has done in Ontario in terms of trying to fight the recession. I want to say to that minister: kids who cannot have food today are not going to be the leaders tomorrow.
Studies have shown that children who have poor food intake are poor students and have the highest dropout rate. They will not be tomorrow's leaders. We have to recognize that we have to do things today as well as think about tomorrow.
I am not saying it is any one policy, but it is that whole range of taxes and deregulation and free trade and the psychological aspect. Owner-operator truckers have no breaks whatsoever. They cannot get welfare because they have got this asset called a rig. If they want to get welfare they can sell the rig, if somebody would buy it, but then they have no livelihood, no chance. Because they are an independent operation they do not qualify for unemployment insurance.
They would be more than happy to pay unemployment insurance premiums if they could qualify.
As it stands, when times are tough it is their life-long, hard-earned savings they have to draw on in order to keep the mortgage payments up on the rig. I will not call them loan payments. They are a mortgage payment, there is no question about it, to provide a roof over their heads and food on the table.
Some of the truckers I have talked to have been losing those homes, are in danger of losing those rigs. One fellow told me this afternoon that he has had to dip into
Supply
his son's educational savings, money he set aside so that his son could go to university some day. They have had to dip into those savings in order to make ends meet today.
They cannot wait for June for these studies to be completed. In fact, when the minister of state was speaking she made reference to the studies becoming public. I hoped that what she meant was that in this House today, either she or the minister will table them so they could be distributed appropriately and we could all have copies. If not, hopefully, within the next two or three days that can happen.
These people want to work for a living. They are not looking for hand-outs. They are looking for some breaks.
It boggled my mind when one fellow told me that when he blew the motor in his rig, the money he spent to buy a new motor was classified as a capital gain and he was taxed accordingly. Does that make sense? A capital gain to replace an engine that blew. I gather that the folks at finance said it was an improvement to his vehicle. That improvement cost him two or three years of payments.
The truckers themselves have asked for a number of solutions, dealing with everything from capital depreciation to both provincial and federal excise taxes to the federal government following the leadership of Ed Philip in Ontario by putting a moratorium on new licences within the federal jurisdiction, particularly those from the United States. They want American truckers to start paying the same taxes in Canada Canadian truckers have to pay.
Maybe the minister of state is right when she said that when they examined it they found it to be a negligible amount. It may very well be, but it is still unfair. It is unfair that an American company who hires American workers to operate American-built rigs to carry American products into Canada can do so without contributing one red cent to the operations of the Government of Canada which provides services to the trucking industry.
It is a question of fairness. Fairness in taxation; fairness in how the truckers are treated. Also, the cabotage. The minister of state referred to the number of checks they have done and the number of people found in violation. However, it is a psychological threat. The word gets out in the industry and it becomes very real in terms of its impact on cargoes.

May 17, 1991
Supply
When truckers are fighting for nickels and dimes because there are too many truckers and too few cargoes they look for every nickel and dime they can find because that is their livelihood. That is their way of putting food on the table. These folks are hurting.
We have seen some action from the provincial level. The provincial government of Ontario did put on a moratorium. It indicated it would control the brokers, licence them and bond them. That is one of the measures the truckers have been calling for.
I am not going to deny that the Ontario government raised the fuel tax. This government also has to accept the fact that in the over-all scheme of things the fuel tax component is only one part of the equation.
Yes, it needs to be dealt with, but so does the write-off, the capital depreciation, so does unfair competition, so does deregulation. Those items have to be addressed as well and they have to be addressed quickly.
Earlier today the Minister of Transport for Ontario, Ed Philip, wrote to the federal Minister of Transport. My understanding is that his letter has now been released publicly but that the federal minister's response has not yet been completed and made available. I would not mind in the question and comment period if the minister would respond.
Just by way of background, Ed Philip and I first worked together as members of the Ontario legislature. One of the things that we did was participate in the Select Committee on the Highway Transportation of Goods back in 1976-77, which was the first Ontario study of trucking deregulation. We said back then to Ontario: "Don't do it". Just like my colleague for Regina-Lums-den and I said in this House on the white paper Freedom to Move, as well as the NTA and companion legislation, "Don't deregulate trucking or rail or air like you are going to". It is an issue that Ed Philip and I have been involved in for many, many years, fighting to protect the workers in the province of Ontario and in Canada.
I would like to read into the record Ed Philip's letter of May 16:
1 am writing with regards to the current situation facing Ontario's tracking industry. As you know, the activities of the past few days have brought the plight of the trucking industry and the desperation of many individual truckers into clear focus. I believe it is incumbent upon you and I to take the representations of the truckers very seriously.
I met with two delegations of truckers yesterday, and discussed with them the measures that Ontario has already taken to begin to address the problems in the industry. They understood, however, that Ontario's role is limited in that the basic problems-an oversupply of trucking capacity as a result of deregulation, and competition with U.S. trucking companies due to free trade and other federal economic policies-are clearly within federal jurisdiction. I assured them that I would contact you to raise these concerns on their behalf.
You will know, Ontario has already taken measures to begin to address the problems in the trucking industry. We have, for example, announced a moratorium on the issuance of operating authorities under the Thick Transportation Act. We have announced our intention to license and require bonding for load brokers. We have increased enforcement to ensure compliance with provincial regulations. In addition, we are nearing completion of an in-depth study of trans-border competitiveness issues, which will provide us with a base to assess all cost factors relating to U.S.-Ontario competition.
I realize you are also undertaking a number of studies, but I feel it is also of vital importance that you give some indication of support for the plight of the truckers by announcing measures similar to those taken by Ontario. In particular, an announcement of a moratorium on interprovincial and trans-border trucking licenses should be made immediately, to arrest the precipitous decline of the Canadian tracking industry.
I am prepared to meet with you as soon as it can be arranged to discuss these matters further. You and I have a responsibility to explore all avenues which will help to stabilize and ultimately to restore the financial viability of Ontario's and Canada's trucking industry. I will not sit by while this industry goes under, and I believe you will not either. I look forward to meeting you soon.
Sincerely,
Ed Philip,
Minister.
I would echo that appeal for the federal government to, at the very least, place a moratorium on interprovincial and trans-border trucking licences. I think, based on the comments by the Minister of State for Transport, there may be some willingness by the government to do it because of her comments about how awful it was that so many new licences were issued in Ontario in the last six months.
Ontario recognized that they had to find a solution to that problem and the two-year moratorium was part of that solution. I would encourage the government to continue on.
I would also encourage the government to continue, as I know it is doing today, its meetings between officials of the department and representatives of the truckers. Only through that mechanism can the government
May 17, 1991

understand the impact on these human beings and the transportation economy of this country.
I want to take my last couple of minutes to return to what I said at the beginning. This is not just about trucking. This is not just about transportation. This is about real anger out there at the direction in which this country is going. There is a real feeling that we are being tom apart.
Instead of the east-west linkage that Sir John A. Macdonald built in this country, starting with the Canadian Pacific Railway, we have too much north-south. When the truckers argue that they are being unfairly competed against by the American truckers, that is part and parcel of what other Canadians are feeling.
I spent the last 10 days before the House resumed holding a series of working sessions in my riding, particularly in the rural part, to ask people to draft their own throne speech and to give us the agenda items for the Government of Canada.
One thing came out of that totally unprompted. All I asked was: "What do you want Canada to do for your community, for your family, your province, your country and/or your planet?" That is the only question that I put to them. Time and time again they said: "It is as if we woke up one morning and the country was different. We lost the things that linked us together such as VIA Rail, CBC, Canada Post and those kinds of institutions".
They were crying out in anger because they did not like the way this country was being changed. They were afraid they were going to be forced to become American when all our lives we wanted to be different.
We wanted to be Canadians. They are prepared to pay the price to do that. There is no question about it. They recognize that those kinds of things do not come cheap. They recognize that in a perfect world, the north-south linkages would fit the market model.
Canada does not fit the market model. This government does not understand that. This government does not understand that there is a reason why Canada should exist separately from the United States. The only way we can do that is by having east-west transportation linkages, by having viable transportation entities in this
Supply
country whether that means trucking, rail, air or marine. We have to be able to have our own.
At the rate we are going, at the level of bankruptcies we have seen, and at the rate of movement of trucking companies to the United States, we are not going to have our own domestic truck industry in this country.
We will have to rely on somebody else's trucks regulated by somebody else, controlled and owned by somebody else, driven by somebody else and with not one Canadian, perhaps other than a dispatcher or a broker, having any kind of employment related to the trucking industry.
It is time this government woke up to the fact that it has been taking this country in the wrong direction. We have to go east-west, not north-south. That is why we have to find solutions to the trucking problem, as well as the other problems that ail this country which were created by this government.

Madam Speaker, I want to begin my remarks by saying that I have no doubt of the compassion in the mind and heart of the hon. junior minister of transport. I have no doubt whatsoever.
Unfortunately, the Canadian people and the truckers in particular have some doubts. The reason they have doubts is because actions speak louder than words.
Since Monday we have seen in this city of Ottawa and, on our television sets, in and around Toronto on Highway 401 the manifestation of the frustration, the anger and the fear of the truck drivers who are being forced out of existence and are losing their livelihood in this country. This morning I met with a some of the wives and children of these truckers. I saw the apprehension on the faces of the women who understood what the future held for them and it was not very pretty. I saw the faces of the children who did not understand. They only knew that their parents were frightened and that something was terribly wrong.
This is something that those of us in Atlantic Canada can understand and empathize with all too well. We have seen in Atlantic Canada so much of the infrastructure that makes us competitive and even faintly prosperous as Canadians go the way of extinction. In Atlantic Canada we are losing our trains. Our highways are in abysmal shape. Our great ports, most particularly in the city that I

May 17, 1991
Supply
have the great honour to represent, the city of Halifax, are in danger of shutting down and the Minister of Transport knows this and knows it well.
We know all these things are taking place and we know why these things are taking place. They are taking place because of an absolutely overblown, over-optimistic, and overbearing belief in the survival of the fittest and the somehow deity-given right of the free market to control all our lives.
This is not something that is easily recognizable to Canadians in our 124-year history. Canada is the second largest country in the world with an amazing geography. We have somewhere in the vicinity of 27 million people strung across this huge expanse of country. We are located next to one of the largest, richest, most competitive, and most populous countries on the face of the earth. All of those things drive Canadians into a different mode from our neighbours to the south. They have to. We cannot survive. We certainly cannot survive as a country if we opt for the American free market spirit. It will not work here. It cannot work here. It has not worked here, and it does not work here.
With regard to the trucking industry in particular, the industry was deregulated in 1988 before the free trade agreement. We heard the Minister for International Trade come in and make all kinds of comments about how free trade had nothing to do with the problems in this country. I have no comment to make about that. The Canadian people will and have judged on that already.
The deregulation of the trucking industry fell absolutely within the purview of this theory of free market and survival of the fittest. What has happened? We do not have the survival of anybody. The trucking industry, the Canadian trucking industry, is dying. That is why Wellington Street is choked with trucks. That is why Highway 401 was choked with trucks. That is why those people came and met with the Liberal caucus on Monday. That is why those women were here yesterday meeting with my leader and today meeting with other members of the Liberal caucus.
The fittest who survive in Canada now in the trucking industry are Americans.
It is a wonderful country to the south and I wish it well, but let Americans go survive in their own country. Do not let them survive on the basis of a Canadian government that says: "You have every bit as much right to work and prosper in our country as you do in your own". That is not Canadian. That is not the way we do things. That is not what we expect.
Under deregulation this government tells us that anyone who has a truck can operate and anyone can work. Well sometimes the arguments that we present in this House are somewhat confusing to the Canadian people. There is one argument that people understand and that is prices. They understand the difference between prices in Canada and prices in the United States. Our border towns are in great suffering because of cross-border shopping.
I saw in the paper just last week that a mayor of a New York town wanted to nominate the Prime Minister for man of the year in his town because of what he had done for the economy for upper New York state.
I am sure that the minister of fisheries would agree with me on what happens when you tell Canadians about changes in gas prices. Look at the difference in gas prices for these truckers between Canada and the United States. I heard the Minister of Transport and other members on the government side say that the subsidy is higher in Canada. Well, with the greatest of respect, as we would say back home, big deal. The subsidy may be higher in Canada, but the prices are so much lower in the United States that effectively it is almost one-half the cost to fill your tank in the U.S. than in Canada.
How can we expect our truckers to survive in this atmosphere? We cannot. That is why they are out there. That is why they have been here this week and they deserve better than they have been getting from this government. Pious words like "we are full of compassion, we care about Canadians" are not going to do anything for them. They are not going to put food on the tables of these people or shoes on their children's feet. These words are not going pay their mortgages. Decent work is going to pay their mortgages, the ability to compete in what is one of the most superb countries-if

Supply
not the most superb country-in the world, if we run it the way it has to be run.
This is not the United States of America. We do not have 280 million people. We have 27 million people and we have to deal with what we have. We are happy that we only have 27 million people. We do not have the concomitant problems that we would have if we had these huge populations.
If you tie the hands of Canadian truckers, if you tie the hands of Canadian workers, prosperity will become a myth. It has become a myth in the bankruptcies that have taken place and in the number of people unemployed. Worst of all, it has become a myth in the minds of Canadians who look at this government and see no compassion, no assistance, and most of all, no hope.

Madam Speaker, I have a few words on this particular issue. If you know the geography of this country you will realize that Newfoundland is not on the border between the United States and Canada directly in the same sense that a community like Kingston and the Islands does, for instance, or like some of those communities right along the parallel.
Nevertheless, this is an issue that affects us too. It affects us in Newfoundland and it affects us as Canadians generally. I want to say in the limited time available this afternoon that, as a person who arrives on Parliament Hill every morning and who leaves it every night, I have been rather impressed with the way the truckers have conducted their demonstration. It seems to me they ought to be an example for others. They have managed to do things that many demonstrations have failed to do. They have managed to be effective, and certainly that has to be the purpose of any demonstration of that sort. They managed to get the message across, to get the public's attention both across the country and here, in particular terms, to the attention of the decision makers, including the Minister of Transport, whom I am pleased to see in his place at this time.
They have managed to do it with minimum of aggravation. They have parked their rigs but the traffic flow has not been unduly interrupted. I congratulate them, because they got their message across in spades in a very responsible way.
I was out chatting with some of the truckers in the last few days and was overhearing some of their conversations and I was very impressed in terms of the focus they have brought to this particular issue. I thank them and their families on behalf of other members for the way in which they have focused this issue. It is high time somebody focused on this issue. This issue is only the tip of the iceberg of a larger issue: how a number of initiatives of this government are leading us as lambs to the slaughter. It is terrifying, terrifying if you are a truck driver, a consumer or a worker. Nobody is immune it seems to the wrecking ball of this particular government.
The thing that has astounded me as a Canadian in the past few days is to hear the clinical, detached view being mouthed by the Minister of Transport in Question Period and in this debate today by his Minister of State, and by other ministers of the Crown who in clinical fashion think we are dealing somehow with how to perform some remote operation on some inanimate object literally millions of miles away from us. We are talking about real people here, we are talking about people who are losing their rigs, who have lost their bank accounts, who see their livelihood go down the drain, who cannot meet payments and who cannot buy the groceries. We are talking about real live issues here.
It is aggravating for me as an ordinary human being to sit here and to watch the television when I am out in the lobby and to hear members of that crowd over there talk about it as though somehow it is a game of Monopoly or something. I wish to God they would realize the damage that their policies are doing. It is frightful. Do they realize that they, the cabinet ministers and the members of that Tory caucus, are themselves being led as lambs to the slaughter? Do they realize that?
The Prime Minister knows full well what he has unleashed with his series of policies. When he came to government he came for a particular purpose, as we all did, except his purpose is a lot more diabolical than yours could ever be, Madam Speaker, or mine or almost anybody else's in this House. He came to continue what he had done so well in Labrador City. His test plan, his lab operation was called Schefferville, and he did such a job of devastating that he then took his formula to the country as a whole. He is now doing to the country what he did to Schefferville. He is now doing it through the free trade agreement, through deregulation and through other initiatives. He is now affecting his poison. He is now pursuing exactly his agenda of making us a poor cousin of the Americans, of making us the fifty-first state

economically and of making us an appendage economically. That has been his agenda from day one.
You look at his initiatives and they are all aimed that way. If you spent your corporate life and your business life taking orders from Cleveland, it is not difficult to get used to taking orders from Washington.
The minister can shrug and can put on the old bluff and pretend "My leader, right or wrong." He can do that all he wants, he does not understand what I am talking about because he is not from Newfoundland and he was not one of the people who got the axe in Schefferville. He would not know. He has to believe that his man from Baie Comeau has got some principle left. Well, I have news for him. I have got news for him. If that person from Baie Comeau had any principle left he would not be doing this to the people of this country, he would not be doing this to the truckers of this country. You do yourself a disservice in defending that kind of skulduggery. You do yourself a disservice. I thought better of you than that. I never thought of you as a clown, I never thought of you as a puppet.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Stupid little fella.

Ah, we hear it. This is the minister who is going to solve the truckers' problems. This is the minister who wants to bring "cerebral approaches" to the solution, this is the man who wants to rise above it all.
Let me repeat for you, Madam Speaker, because I am sure you missed it. He just called me a stupid little fella. That is his idea of a debate. No wonder he finds himself defending the indefensible, defending the guy from Baie Comeau who wants to sell us, lock, stock and barrel, to the United States.
Who wants to destroy Canada? You say I want to destroy Canada? Am I the person running the truckers into the ground? The minister and his Prime Minister are the ones-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It being four o'clock p.m.-
Let him finish.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There was a question at one point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. There was not agreement. What was said was: "Let's see how much time there is left."
Actually, if time had to be given to us, there would be actually a minute and a half left to the hon. member's 10 minutes.
The hon. member for York West was rising?

Madam Speaker, the hon. member from Thunder Bay said that if there is no question and answer, there may be time to get both speakers in.
I know he used the word "may". I think we took him in good faith. I know my colleague was simply wrapping up. If you would accord him the extra minute that he needs to finish this debate, I would appreciate it, given the fact that we did change the procedure. We are playing by your rules, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We did not change procedure. Is there unanimous consent to give the hon. member an extra minute and a half to complete his remarks?
Agreed.
No.

Unanimous consent has just been withdrawn.
